6. Analysis of downregulation/overexpression of TOX3 by RNAscope is rather
qualitative. Other quantitative methods should be included.
Response：Thank you for the suggestion to include additional quantitative methods. In
response, we have performed the following supplemental analyses:
For the AAV-mediated Tox3 overexpression model, in addition to the RNAscope
analysis confirming specificity and successful overexpression (Figure R1.1b), we had
already provided qPCR data from hypothalamic tissues in our original submission
(see Figure S6b in the revised manuscript) (Figure R1.4a). This qPCR result confirms
a significant increase in Tox3 mRNA levels in mice injected with AAV-Tox3
compared with controls, providing direct quantitative evidence of transcript-level
overexpression.
Regarding the sparse, POMC-neuron-specific knockout model, bulk-tissue qPCR is
technically challenging due to profound signal dilution, as POMC neurons constitute
only a minute fraction of the total hypothalamic population7. Therefore, our validation
relied on RNAscope combined with a tdTomato reporter to visualize gene expression
specifically within the targeted neurons—an approach commonly employed in the
field for similar studies on sparse neuronal populations including POMC neurons1, 8.
We have now performed a quantitative re-analysis of the RNAscope images. Using
ImageJ, we quantified Tox3 mRNA fluorescence intensity specifically within
tdTomato+ POMC neurons and tdTomato- cells. This analysis confirms a significant
reduction in Tox3 mRNA signal in knockout neurons compared with controls, but not
in other cells (Figure R1.4b-d), as well as in HFD-fed Pomc-cre;Ai9 mice relative to
CD-fed controls (Figure R1.4e-g). We have updated these quantitative results in our
revised manuscript.

9. Concerning the snRNAseq data: in Suppl Figure 11C, by looking at the UMAP

indeed an important point we had previously overlooked, and we sincerely appreciate
the reviewer bringing it to our attention. To directly address this question and
distinguish between a genuine biological difference and potential individual sample
variability, we expanded the study by increasing the number of snRNA-seq biological

10. Data in cell lines: did authors check for expression of POMC in the cell lines used?
GT1-7 cells do not express POMC, but are known model for GnRH neurons. Same
for N2a cells, they are known to not express POMC endogenously.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful and technically precise
comment regarding the cell lines used in our study.
The reviewer is correct that GT1-7 cells are primarily a model for GnRH neurons,
while N2a cells are a neuroblastoma line; neither is a canonical, high-fidelity model
for mature POMC neurons. Our own qPCR analysis did detect low or modest levels
of endogenous Pomc expression in both lines (Ct ~29 in GT1-7; Ct ~24 in N2a).
This reflects a broader technical limitation in the field of hypothalamic neurobiology:
well-characterized, faithful in vitro models of specific neuronal populations, such as
POMC neurons, remain scarce. In the absence of such ideal systems, established
neuronal cell lines have been employed in prior studies1, 9 to dissect molecular
mechanisms relevant to hypothalamic signaling pathways-including those central to
our investigation-providing a precedent for their use in this context.
While not a perfect surrogate, these models allowed us to perform controlled
mechanistic studies of the TOX3-PTEN-AKT axis in a neuronal setting. We have
added the following statements in the revised manuscript to explicitly acknowledge
this limitation: Furthermore, the lack of ideal cellular models that faithfully
recapitulate POMC neurons remains a limitation in the field. Although GT1-7 and
N2a cells have been used in prior studies1, 9 and in the present study as in vitro models
for POMC research, neither fully recapitulates the molecular profile of mature POMC
neurons. Future studies would benefit from developing more physiologically relevant
systems—such as POMC-enriched cell lines or hypothalamic organoids—to better
model cell-autonomous mechanisms in these neurons.
11. Statistical analyses: authors state they used one way ANOVA, but for several
analysis they need to carry out either repeated ANOVAs (time is a factor, together
with genotype) or 2 way ANOVAs (genotypes and diets or treatments as factors).
Response: We thank the reviewer for this critical and accurate comment regarding our
statistical analysis. In response, we have systematically reanalyzed all relevant
datasets (including body weight curves, GTTs, ITTs, rectal/interscapular temperature,
indirect calorimetry data, and other experiments with multiple factors) using the
correct statistical models, followed by appropriate post hoc tests where applicable.
We have comprehensively updated the manuscript to reflect these corrections. The
Statistical Analysis section in the Methods has been revised to accurately describe the
application of these models: Significance was determined by two-way analysis of
variance (ANOVA) with Sidak’s multiple comparisons test, unpaired two-tailed
Student’s t test, and one-way ANOVA with post-hoc Tukey’s test as specified in the
figure legends.
12. Are Tox3 flox mice characterized? Are there data showing the model works
properly?
Response: Thank you for raising this important point regarding the characterization of
the Tox3-flox mouse model.
The Tox3-flox mouse line used in our study was kindly provided by Prof. Tao Huang
at Shandong University. In our colony, all mice were rigorously genotyped via
standard PCR on tail DNA to confirm the presence of the correctly inserted loxP sites
flanking the critical exons of the Tox3 gene (representative results are shown in
Figure R1.8a), ensuring the integrity of the floxed allele. Corresponding
representative genotyping results for the Pomc-Cre mice are also provided (Figure
R1.8b). These new data have been incorporated into the revised manuscript.
Crucially, the functionality of this specific floxed allele has been previously validated.
The originating laboratory has demonstrated that this same mouse line, when crossed
with an Albumin-Cre driver, results in a hepatocyte-specific knockout with a clear and
expected metabolic phenotype (e.g., altered hepatic gluconeogenesis)10. This prior
independent application confirms that the Tox3-flox allele is functional and that
Cre-mediated recombination effectively generates a null allele.
Therefore, the Tox3-flox model used here is both genotypically verified in our
laboratory and has been functionally validated in prior work, robustly supporting its
suitability for our conditional knockout approach.

Reviewer #2
While obesity and related metabolic disorders such as type 2 diabetes and fatty liver
disease have become a growing public health concern, the molecular mechanisms
controlling central energy balance remain incompletely understood. Previous studies
established that the hypothalamus, particularly pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC)
neurons in the arcuate nucleus, a first-order metabolic sensor, serves as a central
regulator of energy homeostasis. In this study, the authors identified thymocyte
selection-associated high mobility group box 3 (TOX3) as a key transcriptional
co-regulator in hypothalamic POMC neurons. By utilizing cell-type specific genetic
mouse models, the authors demonstrated that conditional deletion of TOX3 in POMC
neurons exacerbates high-fat diet (HFD)–induced obesity, adipocyte hypertrophy,
hepatic steatosis, and insulin resistance, whereas TOX3 overexpression protects mice
against these metabolic abnormalities. Indirect calorimetry and thermography results
revealed that TOX3 enhanced adipose tissue metabolism and energy expenditure
through stimulating sympathetic outflow to adipose tissue, promoting lipolysis and
brown adipose thermogenesis. Mechanistically, they identified a novel regulatory
effect of TOX3 in proteasomal degradation of PTEN, leading to enhanced AKT
signaling and increased POMC neuronal activity. Meanwhile, similar manipulations
in agouti-related peptide (AgRP) neurons showed no significant metabolic effects.
Although TOX3 has been previously implicated in metabolic disorders, this study
newly identifies hypothalamic TOX3, specifically within POMC neurons, as a key
regulator of energy homeostasis. And this effect is mediated through the TOX3–
PTEN–AKT signaling axis. The data are rather comprehensive. There are several
issues the authors should address to improve the manuscript.
Response: We thank you for the positive assessment of our study on hypothalamic
TOX3 in energy homeostasis via POMC neurons. Your constructive feedback is
highly valuable. In response, we have conducted additional experiments, analyses,
and revisions to address each point directly. Below, we provide point-by-point
responses and outline the changes made in the revised manuscript.
Specific comments:
1. The title of the manuscript is somewhat vague. It would be better if the authors
would revise it and improve the clarity. A suggested title is “TOX3 in hypothalamic
POMC neurons improves adipose tissue energy homeostasis by targeting PTEN–AKT
signaling axis.”
Response: Thank you for the helpful suggestion to improve the manuscript title. In
response, we have revised the title to: “TOX3 in hypothalamic POMC neurons
regulates energy balance via the PTEN-AKT signaling axis” to accurately and
concisely captures a central mechanistic finding of our study. We believe this change
significantly enhances the clarity and focus of our manuscript, and we sincerely
appreciate this constructive recommendation.
2. The authors examined the TOX3 mRNA expression across various mouse tissues
and cell types using qPCR and RNAscope. It would strengthen the study if they also
verified TOX3 distribution using available single-cell RNA sequencing databases to
confirm TOX3 distribution across tissues and neuronal cell types.
Response: Thank you for this excellent suggestion. As suggested, we have analyzed
publicly available datasets.
First, examination of bulk RNA-seq data across tissues (PRJCA019393) confirmed
that Tox3 mRNA expression is significantly higher in the brain compared to peripheral
tissues (Figure R2.1a), consistent with our initial qPCR results (see Supplementary
Figure 1a). To achieve higher resolution, we then examined Tox3 expression across
different brain regions. This analysis revealed that Tox3 expression levels are highest
in the hypothalamus, being significantly higher than those in the thalamus,
hippocampus, and cortex (Figure R2.1b).
Most importantly, as suggested, we interrogated existing mouse hypothalamic
scRNA-seq datasets (GSE188646). These data robustly corroborated our RNAscope
findings, demonstrating that Tox3 expression is predominantly enriched in neuronal
populations, with minimal expressions in astrocytes, tanycytes, and microglia (Figure
R2.1c,d). An interesting additional observation was unexpectedly high Tox3
expression in oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) (Figure R2.1d), which hints at
a potential novel role for TOX3 in OPC biology, a point we have discussed in the
revised Discussion section.
We have integrated these new analyses into the revised manuscript, presenting them in
the Results section and as new Fig. 1a-d.
Figure R2.1 (a) Tox3 expression profile across different tissues by analyzing bulk
RNAseq dataset (PRJCA019393). (b) qPCR analysis of Tox3 mRNA expression
across different brain regions of wild-type C57BL/6J mice (n=3). (c) UMAP plot
showing the clustering of cell types in the hypothalamus by analyzing public

3. In addition to comparing TOX3 levels between chow diet–fed and high-fat diet–fed
mice, the authors can incorporate analysis of relevant human datasets to enhance the
clinical relevance. If the human datasets are not available, the limitation should be
clearly discussed.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the valuable suggestion to enhance the clinical
relevance of our findings. We have thoroughly searched relevant public datasets but
were unable to identify human data that directly compare TOX3 expression in the
brain under different dietary conditions. We have therefore explicitly acknowledged
this as a current limitation in the Discussion section of the revised manuscript as
follows: Finally, while our murine models have provided mechanistic insights into
TOX3's role in POMC neurons, we note that direct evidence linking TOX3 expression
to obesity in humans is currently unavailable. Future studies that incorporate human
datasets or relevant physiological models, such as hypothalamic organoids derived
from human pluripotent stem cells, would help establish the translational relevance of
this pathway in human energy homeostasis.
4. In Supplementary Figure 2A, most TOX3 signals appear to be located outside
POMC neurons, and high-fat diet treatment does not seem to significantly reduce
TOX3 expression, which seems to be inconsistent with the results shown in Figure 1D.
The rationale of focusing on POMC neuron–specific TOX3 should be better
elaborated.
Response: Thank you for your insightful comment.
To address the concern directly, we have replaced the original image in
Supplementary Figure 2A with a more representative one and performed new
quantitative analysis using ImageJ. This re-analysis specifically measured Tox3
mRNA fluorescence intensity within POMC (tdTomato-positive) neurons. The results
confirm a significant reduction in Tox3 signal in POMC neurons under high-fat diet
(HFD) compared to chow diet (CD) (Figure R2.2a,b).
We fully agree with the reviewer’s observation that Tox3 is also expressed in other
cell types within the ARC, as evidenced by signal in tdTomato-negative cells.
Quantitative analysis of these non-POMC cells indeed shows a modest, though less
pronounced, decrease under HFD (Figure R2.2c). This finding, together with the
whole-hypothalamus data in Figure 1D, supports that Tox3 expression is not exclusive
to POMC neurons but is more widespread in the hypothalamus. We acknowledge that
we cannot exclude a functional role for TOX3 in other neuronal populations or
regions.
Figure R2.2 (a) Representative confocal images of POMC (tdTomato+, green), Tox3
(red), and DAPI (blue) in the ARC of Pomc-cre;Ai9 male mice fed a standard CD or
HFD for 16 weeks. Scale bar, 50 μm. Integrated density quantification of Tox3 in
tdTomato+ (b) and tdTomato- (c) neurons from (a).
Our decision to focus on POMC (and AgRP) neurons stems from several established
considerations: (1) our preliminary data showed that hypothalamic Tox3 knockdown
disrupts whole-body energy homeostasis; (2) the ARC is a key hypothalamic nucleus
for metabolic regulation; and (3) POMC and AgRP neurons represent the two primary,
antagonistic populations within the ARC that centrally coordinate energy balance12, 13,
14. Studying TOX3 in these well-defined, metabolically critical neurons provides a
clear and physiologically relevant model to dissect its cell-type-specific role.
We have incorporated the following statements in the Discussion section of our
revised manuscript: First, although we have comprehensively characterized TOX3
expression and function in POMC and AgRP neurons, it is also expressed in other
hypothalamic neuronal populations. Moreover, while minimal Tox3 expression was
detected in tanycytes, astrocytes, and microglia, public scRNA-seq datasets indicate
that Tox3 is enriched in oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs), suggesting a
potential role in glial biology. The physiological relevance of TOX3 in these other
neuronal and non-neuronal cell types, particularly under metabolic challenge,
represents an important avenue for future research.
5. The degree of obesity differs between the loss-of-function and gain-of-function
experiments. The control group in the gain-of-function study (Control) appears more
obese than the LoxP control group in the loss-of-function study, with higher body
weight, liver weight, and more fat tissue. Please explain this inconsistency.
Response: Thank you for raising this important observation regarding the baseline
adiposity differences between the control groups in our loss-of-function and
gain-of-function studies. We appreciate the opportunity to clarify this point.
The apparent discrepancy arises primarily from the distinct experimental designs,
especially the timing of high-fat diet (HFD) initiation relative to the intervention.
In the loss-of-function study, both LoxP and PTKO mice began HFD at 6 weeks of age
and remained on the diet for 12 weeks. In contrast, in the gain-of-function study,
Pomc-Cre mice underwent an 8-week HFD pre-feeding period to establish
obesity before AAV-mediated TOX3 overexpression (or control). After intervention,
they continued HFD for another 12 weeks. As a result, the control group in the
gain-of-function study had already accumulated 8 weeks of HFD-induced weight gain
prior to the experimental comparison, naturally leading to higher baseline adiposity,
liver weight, and body weight than the controls in the loss-of-function study.
Additionally, the two studies used independent cohorts of mice with different genetic
backgrounds (Tox3flox/flox controls vs. Pomc-Cre controls), bred and maintained at
different times. While diet and housing conditions were standardized, some
inter-cohort variability in the severity of diet-induced obesity is common and can
influence absolute metabolic parameters.
Thus, the difference in control phenotypes is not an inconsistency but a logical
outcome of the distinct experimental timelines and cohorts. The central and consistent
finding across both studies remains clear: reducing TOX3 exacerbates obesity, while
increasing it confers protection—each relative to its internally matched control group.
We have clarified these methodological details in the revised manuscript to ensure
transparency.
6. The study proposes that TOX3 in POMC neurons regulates adipose tissue
metabolism through sympathetic nervous system modulation. In addition to assessing
NE content and turnover, the authors should also examine the expression levels of
β-adrenergic receptors in adipose tissues to support this mechanistic claim.
Response: Thank you for raising this insightful suggestion, which prompted us to
strengthen our mechanistic analysis. As suggested, we have conducted qPCR analysis
to examine the mRNA expression levels of β-adrenergic receptors (Adrβ1, Adrβ2, and
Adrβ3) in eWAT, iWAT, and BAT.
Our new data reveal that TOX3 in POMC neurons orchestrates a coordinated
regulation of both sympathetic tone and target tissue sensitivity. In PTKO mice, the
reduction in BAT NE levels and turnover was accompanied by a downregulation of
Adrβ1, Adrβ2, and Adrβ3 mRNA (Figure R2.3c). Conversely, TOX3 overexpression
(PTOE) increased Adrβ2 and Adrβ3 mRNA expression (Figure R2.3f). These
findings demonstrate that the TOX3-POMC axis likely modulates not only
neurotransmitter availability but also the adrenergic responsiveness of the target tissue.
Notably, β-adrenergic receptor expression remained unchanged in eWAT and iWAT
(Figure R2.3a,b; 3d,e), highlighting the specificity of this regulation to BAT.
Together with our functional rescue experiment using a β3-AR selective agonist
(Figure 5f-k), these results establish a dual-level mechanism: TOX3 in POMC
neurons maintains both the sympathetic drive to BAT and the intrinsic adrenergic
signaling capacity of the tissue itself. These data have been incorporated into the
revised manuscript.
Figure R2.3 qPCR analysis of the mRNA expression levels of β-adrenergic receptors
in eWAT (n=5:5) (a), iWAT (n=5:5) (b), and BAT (n=9:5) (c) of HFD-fed LoxP and
PTKO mice. qPCR analysis of the mRNA expression levels of β-adrenergic receptors
in eWAT (n=5:5) (d), iWAT (n=5:5) (e), and BAT (n=5:6) (f) of HFD-fed Control and
PTOE mice.
7. The study only confirms the protective role of the sympathetic nervous system in
TOX3-mediated effects in brown adipose tissue (BAT) using 6-hydroxydopamine
hydrobromide (6-OHDA). The authors should also evaluate the effects of sympathetic
inhibition in white adipose tissue (WAT) before concluding that the protective effect is
specifically mediated via BAT.
Response: Thank you for raising this important point, which prompted us to perform
the critical experiment you suggested. To specifically evaluate the role of sympathetic
innervation in WAT, we performed bilateral, local microinjections of 6-OHDA into
both the eWAT and iWAT depots of control and PTOE mice.
The results showed that, following chemical denervation of eWAT and iWAT (Figure
R2.4a-c), PTOE mice continued to exhibit a lower body weight than control mice
(Figure R2.4d), along with reduced fat mass and increased lean mass composition
(Figure R2.4e). Combined with our BAT denervation results, these data provide
strong functional evidence that sympathetic innervation of BAT is the primary and
necessary efferent pathway through which elevated TOX3 in POMC neurons exerts
its protective effect against weight gain.
Figure R2.4 NE content in eWAT (a), iWAT (b), and BAT (c) of Pomc-Cre mice
injected with AAV-GFP or AAV-Tox3, followed by bilateral injection of either saline
or 6-OHDA into both eWAT and iWAT. (d) Body weight of Control and PTOE mice 4
weeks after 6-OHDA injection. (e) Mass composition of Control and PTOE mice 4
weeks after 6-OHDA injection.
It is noteworthy that, although TOX3 overexpression increased NE content in WAT
depots (See Supplementary Figure 10d), the denervation experiment indicates that this
modulation alone is not sufficient to drive the core body weight phenotype under our
experimental conditions. Sympathetic tone to WAT may play a modulatory role but
does not appear to be the dominant mediator of the TOX3-dependent effect on
whole-body energy balance.
Thus, our data supports a model in which TOX3 in POMC neurons preferentially
enhances sympathetic output to BAT. The recruited BAT then acts as the primary
driver of increased energy expenditure, outweighing the relative contribution of
sympathetic-mediated effects in WAT to the overall metabolic phenotype.
We have updated the Methods, Results and Discussion sections to include these new
WAT denervation data and to refine our conclusion accordingly: Notably, although
TOX3 overexpression also increased NE content in WAT depots, sympathetic
denervation experiments indicate that this modulation alone is not sufficient to drive
the core body weight phenotype under our experimental conditions. Thus, while
sympathetic tone to WAT may exert a modulatory role, it does not appear to be the
dominant mediator of TOX3-dpendent regulation of whole-body energy balance.
Instead, our data support a model in which TOX3 in POMC neurons preferentially
enhances sympathetic output to BAT. The BAT then acts as the primary driver of
increased energy expenditure, outweighing the relative contribution of
sympathetic-mediated effects in WAT to the overall metabolic phenotype.
8. The current study focuses on the TOX3/POMC effect on the adipose tissue, but
some of the adipose data were associations, meaning the author cannot exclude the
effect of TOX3/POMC on extra-adipose tissues. The systemic use of β3-adrenergic
agonist also has its limitation in interpreting the adipose phenotype. The authors
should profile the expression of key metabolic genes in the liver and skeletal muscles
to see if there are collateral benefits in these metabolically important extra-adipose
tissues.
Response: Thank you for this insightful suggestion. As recommended, we have
performed qPCR analysis to profile the expression of key metabolic genes in the liver
(Cd36, Srebf1, Fasn, Acaca, Cpt1α, Cpt2, Apob, Mttp) and skeletal muscle (Cd36,
Fabp3, Fatp1, Ucp3, Cpt1α, Acox1, Atp2a1, Atp2a2).
We found that PTKO mice exhibited significantly higher mRNA levels
of Cd36 and Srebf1, together with lower levels of Cpt1α, Apob, and Mttp in the liver
compared to LoxP controls, while no significant changes were observed in skeletal
muscle (Figure R2.5a,b). Conversely, PTOE mice showed downregulated expression
of Cd36, Srebf1, Acaca, and Apob, alongside upregulated Cpt2 in the liver, compared
to controls (Figure R2.5c). Again, no significant alterations were detected in skeletal
muscle (Figure R2.5d). These data have been incorporated in our revised manuscript.
We revised our Discussion section as follows: However, several important questions
remain unanswered, including whether hypothalamic POMC neuron TOX3 directly
modulates other peripheral metabolic processes - such as hepatic gluconeogenesis,
hepatic lipid metabolism, pancreatic endocrine function, and skeletal muscle
metabolism - as well as the molecular mechanisms underlying these potential effects.

Reviewer #3:
The manuscript by Qin Tang, Juan Pang and Jinhang Zhang et al. presents a
compelling and well-designed study that significantly advances the understanding of
central regulation of energy homeostasis. The authors provide robust evidence
identifying TOX3 as a critical and previously overlooked metabolic regulator
specifically within POMC neurons. Using genetic models, the authors show that
TOX3 loss exacerbates diet-induced obesity, while its overexpression improves
metabolism via a post-translational mechanism involving PTEN degradation and
enhanced AKT signaling. The findings reveal a neuron-specific role for TOX3 in
energy homeostasis and suggest its potential as a therapeutic target for metabolic
disorders. However, there are some experiments and descriptions need to be
improved.
Response: Thank you for your constructive review and positive assessment of our
study on TOX3 in POMC neurons and energy homeostasis. Your constructive
feedback is highly valuable. In response, we have conducted additional experiments,
analyses, and revisions to address each point directly. Below, we provide
point-by-point responses and outline the changes made in the revised manuscript.
Major concerns:
1. The authors should discuss the apparent discrepancy wherein POMC
neuron-specific TOX3 ablation shows no phenotype on a chow diet (CD), despite the
significant metabolic effect observed upon broader hypothalamic TOX3 knockdown
under the same conditions. Please clarify whether this suggests that TOX3 in
non-POMC hypothalamic neurons is responsible for the metabolic regulation
observed under CD, and how this aligns with the proposed POMC-specific role for
TOX3.
Response: We appreciate the opportunity to clarify this apparent discrepancy, which
stems from a key difference in the experimental conditions that we may not have
emphasized sufficiently.
The significant metabolic effect following broader hypothalamic Tox3 knockdown
was specifically observed under high-fat diet (HFD) feeding (see Figure 1). In
contrast, the POMC neuron-specific ablation was tested on a CD, where we did not
observe a metabolic phenotype.
However, a critical and consistent finding that further strengthens our conclusion is
that under HFD conditions, the POMC neuron-specific Tox3 knockout (see Figure 2)
recapitulates the key metabolic phenotypes observed with the broader hypothalamic
knockdown. This demonstrates that Tox3 in POMC neurons is both necessary and
sufficient to mediate the metabolic effects observed under dietary challenge.
Therefore, the absence of a phenotype in the POMC-specific KO mice on CD cannot
be directly compared to the effects of global hypothalamic knockdown, as the latter
was assessed under metabolically challenged (HFD) conditions. The cell-type-specific
effects are diet-context dependent. We fully agree that non-POMC hypothalamic
neurons might also be involved in Tox3-dependent metabolic regulation, especially
under dietary stress. This view is consistent with our expression data showing Tox3 in
other neuronal populations (See Figure S2a) and with the known complexity of
hypothalamic energy balance circuits.
We have revised the Discussion to explicitly acknowledge that Tox3 likely functions
in a cell-type- and context-specific manner, and that its role in non-POMC
neurons—particularly under metabolic challenge—deserves future investigation:
although we have comprehensively characterized TOX3 expression and function in
POMC and AgRP neurons, it is also expressed in other hypothalamic neuronal
populations. Moreover, while minimal Tox3 expression was detected in tanycytes,
astrocytes, and microglia, public scRNA-seq datasets indicate that Tox3 is enriched in
oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs), suggesting a potential role in glial biology.
The physiological relevance of TOX3 in these other neuronal and non-neuronal cell
types, particularly under metabolic challenge, represents an important avenue for
future research.
2. It would also be important to know the phenotypic effects of overexpressing TOX3
in POMC neurons under chow diet conditions, to fully elucidate its physiological role
without the confounder of dietary stress.
Response: Thank you for this important suggestion. As suggested, we overexpressed
TOX3 specifically in ARC POMC neurons of Pomc-Cre mice maintained on a
standard chow diet (CD).
Our results showed that, under CD conditions, TOX3 overexpression in POMC
neurons did not significantly affect body weight, body composition (fat and lean
mass), organ weights (liver and adipose depots), serum lipid profiles, glucose
tolerance, or insulin sensitivity (Figure R3.1a-j). This indicates that in the absence of
a metabolic challenge such as a HFD, elevated TOX3 expression in POMC neurons
does not exert a pronounced effect on systemic energy homeostasis. These data have
been included as a Supplementary Figure in the revised manuscript, and the
corresponding Results and figure legends have been updated accordingly.
Figure R3.1 Pomc-Cre mice were bilaterally injected into the ARC with either
AAV-GFP or AAV-Tox3 and maintained on a chow diet (n=5). (a) Body weight curve.
(b) Body weight change curve. (c) Fat mass and lean mass weight. (d) Fat and lean

glucose (h) levels. (i) Glucose tolerance test. (j) Insulin tolerance test.
3. The authors should address the discrepancy between the increased energy
expenditure and the unaffected RER in PTKO mice.
Response: Thank you for your valuable comment. We appreciate the reviewer’s
careful attention of the data. For clarity, the results are as follows: in PTKO mice, we
observed a decrease in energy expenditure alongside unchanged RER. Conversely, in
mice with POMC neuron-specific Tox3 overexpression, we observed an increase in
energy expenditure, also with an unchanged RER.
Thus, the key and consistent finding across both models is that a change in energy
expenditure is not necessarily accompanied by a shift in whole-body fuel preference
(RER). This pattern is physiologically coherent. An unchanged RER indicates stable
proportional oxidation of carbohydrates and fats. The observed alterations in energy
expenditure, therefore, likely reflect changes in basal metabolic rate and/or adaptive
thermogenesis-processes modulated by sympathetic outflow to tissues such as
BAT-rather than a fundamental switch in primary energy substrate or in locomotor
activity. This interpretation is well-supported by our results including BAT
thermogenesis, NE turnover and related data in both models.
We have added the following statement in the Discussion section of our revised
manuscript: Specifically, we observed that TOX3 deletion in POMC neurons
significantly reduced energy expenditure, while its overexpression in hypothalamic
POMC neurons increased it-consistent with the established roles of POMC neurons in
promoting energy dissipation12, 15, 16, 17. Importantly, the RER remained unchanged in
both loss- and gain-of-function models, indicating that the altered energy expenditure
did not result from a shift in whole-body fuel preference. This pattern of metabolic
changes points to alterations in basal metabolic rate and/or adaptive thermogenesis as
the primary driver.
4. Given the reduced thermogenesis in BAT, were there also corresponding changes in
the beiging markers of WAT?
Response: Thank you for raising this important suggestion. As suggested, we
performed qPCR analysis to measure key beiging marker genes in the iWAT of
HFD-fed LoxP and PTKO mice, as well as of HFD-fed Control and PTOE mice.
Our data indicates that neither POMC neuron-specific knockout nor overexpression of
TOX3 significantly altered the expression of these beiging markers in iWAT
(Figure R3.2a,b). This suggests that, under our experimental conditions, the thermogenic
effects mediated by TOX3 in POMC neurons are primarily reflected in BAT function
and do not extend to the beiging process in iWAT. These results have been included in
the revised manuscript.

in iWAT of HFD-fed Control and PTOE mice (n=5).
5. Evidence demonstrating the efficacy of 6-OHDA-mediated sympathetic denervation
(e.g., measurements of tissue norepinephrine levels or tyrosine hydroxylase staining)
should be provided.
Response: Thank you for raising this essential methodological point. As suggested,
we directly measured norepinephrine (NE) content in eWAT, iWAT, and BAT
following targeted 6-OHDA injection into the BAT.
Our results show that NE levels in eWAT and iWAT were not significantly altered by
BAT-localized 6-OHDA injection compared to controls (Figure R3.3a,b). However,
in the targeted BAT depot itself, NE content was significantly reduced in the
6-OHDA-treated group (Figure R3.3c).
These findings confirm both the efficacy of sympathetic denervation within the
injected BAT and its anatomical specificity, as the intervention did not produce
off-target effects in distal white adipose depots. We have incorporated these validation
data into the revised manuscript (Results section) to substantiate the effectiveness and
precision of our denervation approach.

injected with AAV-GFP or AAV-Tox3, followed by injection of saline or 6-OHDA
specifically into the BAT.
Minor concerns:
1. Regarding Figure 6J, it appears that the green fluorescence channel may be missing
from the merged image. This should be clarified or corrected.
Response: Thank you for your careful observation regarding Figure 6J and for
prompting this important clarification.
The reason the green (GFP) channel is not visible in the merged image is intentional,
reflecting the molecular design of our AAV construct. The vector expresses TOX3 and
GFP as separate proteins linked by a P2A self-cleaving sequence. Consequently, while
GFP fluorescence robustly indicates successful viral transduction, it does not report
the subcellular localization of the POMC neurons or TOX3 protein.
The GFP image was originally included only to document transduction efficiency. We
recognize that presenting it alongside the c-FOS signal could inadvertently suggest
co-localization, which is biologically incorrect. To prevent any misinterpretation and
to present the neuronal activation (c-FOS) data with maximum clarity, we have
revised the figure as suggested. The updated Figure 6j now shows only the individual
and merged images of c-FOS immunofluorescence (red) and DAPI (blue), directly
visualizing the activation state of neurons in the relevant region.
2. For the Tox3 in situ hybridization data validating the knockdown efficiency, it is
recommended that representative images be provided that more accurately reflect the
corresponding quantitative results.
Response: Thank you for this suggestion. We have performed additional quantitative
image analysis on the in situ hybridization data to ensure the visual representation
accurately reflects the knockdown efficiency. The results confirm a significant
reduction in Tox3 mRNA signal intensity, consistent with the efficacy of the knockout
(Figure R3.4a,b).
Furthermore, to address any potential concern regarding specificity, we also
quantified Tox3 signal in tdTomato-negative (non-POMC) cells of Pomc-cre;Ai9 and
PTKO;Ai9 mice. The results showed that the knockdown was significant only in
POMC neurons, with no significant difference observed in non-POMC neurons
(Figure R3.4c). These results confirm the cell-type specificity of our approach. These
quantitative results have been included in the revised manuscript.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Dear Reviewers:
Thank you for your letter and for the reviewers’ comments concerning our manuscript entitled “TOX3
in hypothalamic POMC neurons regulates energy balance via the PTEN-AKT signaling axis” (ID:
NCOMMS-25-70758A). These comments are all valuable and very helpful for revising and improving
our paper, as well as guiding our research. We have studied the comments carefully and have made
corrections, hoping they will meet with your approval. The major modifications in the revised
manuscript are tracked in red, and our point-by-point responses to the reviewer’s comments are
provided below:
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have only partly addressed the concerns of this reviewer. The main limitations about the
genetic model used and the approaches to demonstrate deletion/overexpression in mature POMC
neurons still stand.
Concerning the demonstration that the manipulation impact also adult POMC neurons, for figure S2A,
S2F and S6C, instead of using fluorescence of POMC-Cre Ai9 mice, please perform staining for
POMC protein or mRNA in combination with Tox3 mRNA staining. As already mentioned, POMC-
Cre Ai9 label all POMC-lineage cells. The argument used by the authors that other studies have used
this genetic approach to reveal deletion (or overexpression) in POMC cells, does not make the
approach correct.
In the manuscript, it needs to be clear for the reader that the genetic model used does not allow specific
deletion only in POMC neurons. The authors need to consider using terms like POMC-lineage cells
throughout the manuscript.
For the energy expenditure data throughout the manuscript: as there are differences in body weight,
please also use ANCOVA for EE analysis (for details please see PMID: 22205519 and PMID:
34489606).
Response: Thank you for your further insights and for pushing us to address the remaining concerns
regarding our genetic model and data analysis. We appreciate your continued effort to improve the
rigor and clarity of our work. We have carefully revised our manuscript to address all the issues you
have raised.
(1) Regarding the genetic model we used.
We fully acknowledge and agree with your assessment that the POMC-Cre mouse line labels POMC-
lineage cells rather than exclusively mature POMC neurons. While this genetic approach is widely
used in this field, we understand that scientific precision requires accurate terminology that reflects
the true nature of the model. Therefore, as you suggested, we have systematically revised our
manuscript by replacing all instances of “POMC neurons” with “POMC-lineage cells” throughout the
text where we describe our own experimental findings and genetic model. In the Introduction and
Discussion sections, where we discuss general background knowledge and established functions of
POMC neurons based on prior literature, we have retained the term "POMC neurons" as this reflects
the conventional terminology in the field. Additionally, in our snRNA sequencing analysis, we refer to
cells that express Pomc mRNA as "POMC neurons" because this identification is based on actual gene
expression rather than Cre-mediated lineage tracing, which aligns with standard practice in
transcriptomic studies.
We have also substantially expanded the Discussion to explicitly address the POMC-lineage
consideration as follows: “Third, the constitutive Pomc-Cre driver used here targets POMC-lineage
cells rather than exclusively mature POMC neurons, including in extrahypothalamic lineages and
developmental precursors1,2, complicating phenotypic attribution. The observed metabolic phenotypes,
including effects on BAT thermogenesis and obesity development, are consistent with established
functions of hypothalamic POMC neurons in energy balance regulation. However, we cannot
definitively distinguish between contributions from mature POMC neurons and other POMC-lineage
cells within the hypothalamus. While our AAV-based approach achieved adult-onset overexpression
within the ARC, the loss-of-function model still carries the possibility of contributions from Tox3
deletion in off-target cell populations. The development and application of temporally controlled
genetic tools will be necessary to precisely define the adult-specific functions of TOX3 in POMC
neurons.”
We believe these revisions appropriately address your concerns by making clear to readers that our
genetic models target POMC-lineage cells rather than exclusively mature POMC neurons, while
appropriately contextualizing our findings within the established physiological functions of POMC-
expressing neurons.
(2) Regarding energy expenditure data analysis.
Thank you for your insightful suggestion regarding the analysis of energy expenditure data. We
completely agree that ANCOVA is the appropriate method to account for differences in body weight
when evaluating energy expenditure. In fact, we had already performed ANCOVA in our manuscript,
using lean body mass as the covariate, as this is the metabolically more relevant compartment and
aligns with the recommendations in the literature (including PMID: 22205519 and PMID:
34489606)3,4. The results of these analyses are presented in Figure 4b and Figure 4k, and the Methods
section describes the ANCOVA approach as follows: “Differences in the relationship between energy
expenditure and lean body mass were analyzed by analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) with lean body
mass included as a covariate, using the online tool CalR2 (available at CalR2 (calrapp.org))”. We
confirm that the main conclusions regarding energy expenditure remain robust after this adjustment.
We appreciate your attention to rigorous statistical analysis and hope that our revised manuscript meets
your expectations.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
In the revision, the authors have addressed most of my comments and as a result, the manuscript has
improved from its previous version.
A remaining issue is that the authors explained that the difference in the degree of obesity between the
loss-of-function and gain-of-function models is due to the different timing of high-fat diet exposure
relative to the gene manipulation. The authors should clarify the rationale for initiating HFD feeding
before TOX3 overexpression in the gain-of-function model, rather than overexpressing TOX3 prior to
HFD challenge, which would be more comparable with the loss-of-function studies.
Response: Thank you for your positive assessment of our revised manuscript and for your insightful
comment regarding the timing of HFD exposure in our gain-of-function study.
Our gain-of-function model was specifically designed to evaluate the therapeutic potential of TOX3
in the context of established obesity. We therefore first induced obesity by feeding mice HFD for 8
weeks, and then overexpressed TOX3 in the ARC via AAV injection. This approach mimics a clinically
relevant scenario when intervention occurs after obesity has already developed. Importantly, we
observed that endogenous TOX3 expression in POMC-lineage cells is significantly reduced after
prolonged HFD feeding, providing a strong rationale for restoring TOX3 levels specifically in the
obese state.
We acknowledge that this experimental design differs from the loss-of-function studies, where HFD
challenge began at 6 weeks of age. However, the two models address complementary questions: the
loss-of-function model assesses whether endogenous TOX3 is required for normal resistance to diet-
induced obesity, while the gain-of-function model tests whether overexpression of TOX3 can reverse
pre-existing obesity (a therapeutic approach). Despite this difference in timing, the consistent between
loss-of-function and gain-of-function ameliorates provides convergent evidence supporting a critical
role for TOX3 in energy balance regulation.
To clarify this rational for readers, we have revised the Methods section as follows: “To evaluate the
therapeutic potential of TOX3 in the context of established obesity, Pomc-Cre or Agrp-Cre mice were
first fed HFD for 8 weeks to induce obesity, and then anesthetized with isoflurane and received bilateral
stereotaxic injections of either AAV-GFP or AAV-Tox3 vectors into the ARC”.
We agree with the reviewer that overexpressing TOX3 prior to HFD challenge would allow direct
comparison with the loss-of-function model. However, we believe that our current design is
scientifically valid and appropriately tailored to the distinct questions each model was intended to
address. Thank you again for your insightful feedback.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have fully addressed all my previous concerns. I have no further questions and recommend
acceptance.
Response: Thank you very much for your positive assessment and for your valuable contributions
throughout the review process. We are pleased that you find our revisions satisfactory and appreciate
your recommendation for acceptance.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Obesity and its associated metabolic disorders, including type 2 diabetes and fatty liver disease, represent a growing global health burden. Although the hypothalamus is well-established as the central regulator of energy homeostasis through specialized neuronal circuits, the molecular mechanisms governing these pathways remain incompletely elucidated. In this study, we identify thymocyte selection-associated high mobility group box 3 (TOX3) as a critical metabolic regulator in hypothalamic pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC)-lineage cells in mice. By employing cell-type-specific genetic manipulation in murine models, we establish that conditional TOX3 ablation in POMC-lineage cells exacerbates diet-induced obesity and metabolic dysfunction, while its overexpression in these neurons confers robust metabolic benefits. Mechanistically, TOX3 enhances the function of POMC-lineage cells through a post-translational regulatory mechanism involving PTEN proteasomal degradation, leading to potentiated AKT signaling. This central modulation drives sympathetic activation of brown adipose tissues, resulting in enhanced thermogenesis and energy expenditure. Notably, TOX3 exhibits striking neuronal specificity, as both loss- and gain-of-function manipulation in agouti-related peptide (AgRP) neurons produce negligible metabolic consequences. Our work identifies previously unrecognized physiological roles of TOX3 in POMC-lineage cells that are essential for maintaining energy homeostasis in mice, thereby revealing therapeutic opportunities for metabolic disorders.

---

## Introduction

Obesity and its associated metabolic diseases, particularly type 2 diabetes and fatty liver disease, have emerged as a major global health challenge1. Elucidating the intricate mechanisms underlying the pathogenesis of obesity is critical for identifying potential preventive and therapeutic strategies. Fundamentally, obesity results from chronic energy homeostasis disruption due to sustained caloric intake exceeding expenditure2,3. Decades of research have established that energy balance is predominantly regulated by the central nervous system (CNS), with the hypothalamus serving as the central regulatory hub4-6.

The hypothalamic circuitry comprises several well-characterized nuclei, including the arcuate nucleus (ARC), which contains two interlinked but functionally antagonistic neuronal populations: anorexigenic pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) neurons and orexigenic agouti-related peptide (AgRP)/neuropeptide (NPY) neurons6,7. POMC neurons are established as master regulators of negative energy balance, exerting dual control through central suppression of food intake and activation of peripheral sympathetic nervous system (SNS) output-mediated adipose tissue catabolism6,8. Anatomical tracing studies have demonstrated that POMC neurons innervate both white (WAT) and brown adipose tissue (BAT), where norepinephrine (NE) release activates β3-adrenoceptors to stimulate lipolysis in WAT and promote thermogenesis in BAT9-11.

As first-order metabolic sensors, POMC neurons are uniquely positioned to integrate peripheral signals due to their anatomical localization proximity to the median eminence, a circumventricular organ with a fenestrated blood-brain barrier8. This privileged location enables rapid detection of circulating metabolic cues, including nutrients (e.g., glucose, fatty acids) and hormones (e.g., leptin, insulin)6,7. Studies have demonstrated that elevated circulating leptin and insulin triggers a coordinated response in POMC neurons involving acute membrane depolarization and transcriptional upregulation of Pomc and subsequent processing into bioactive peptides5,6,12-14. These adaptations concurrently suppress feeding while enhancing energy expenditure through SNS-mediated adipose tissue remodeling. Importantly, disruption of this regulatory axis-whether through genetic variants, dietary stress, or inflammation-represents a critical node in the pathogenesis of obesity and its metabolic complications4-7.

Thymocyte selection-associated high mobility group box family member 3 (TOX3), a member of the high mobility group box superfamily, functions as an important transcriptional co-regulator15. Human studies and murine models consistently demonstrate predominant TOX3 expression in the brain16,17. In vitro evidence indicates TOX3 regulates calcium-dependent transcription in neurons15, exhibits neuroprotective effects16, and contribute to CNS development16,17, suggesting vital roles in neural physiology. Notably, genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have implicated TOX3 in polycystic ovary syndrome pathogenesis and insulin resistance18. Most recently, TOX3 was identified as a novel regulator of hepatic gluconeogenesis that exacerbates diabetic pathophysiology19, further underscoring its metabolic relevance. However, the precise physiological and pathophysiological roles of TOX3 in metabolic regulation, particularly in energy homeostasis, remain completely unexplored.

Here, we identify TOX3 as a POMC-lineage cell-specific guardian against obesity. Mechanistically, TOX3 expression in hypothalamic POMC-lineage cells promotes phosphatase and tense homolog (PTEN) degradation, enhancing protein kinase B (AKT) signaling to activate sympathetic-driven adipose catabolism. Genetic ablation of TOX3 in POMC-lineage cells exacerbates metabolic dysfunction, whereas its overexpression confers protection, with no significant effects observed in AgRP neurons. These findings position TOX3 as a critical molecular nexus linking hypothalamic signaling to peripheral energy metabolism.

---

## Results

TOX3 is predominantly expressed in hypothalamic neurons
To characterize the expression patterns of TOX3, we first examined its distribution across major metabolic tissues in mice using a publicly available database. Our analysis revealed that Tox3 mRNA expression was most enriched in the brain compared to various peripheral tissues (Fig. 1a). Subsequent qPCR analysis confirmed that Tox3 levels were significantly higher in the hypothalamus than in other brain regions (Fig. 1b) or peripheral tissues (Figure S1a). To determine the cellular localization of TOX3 within hypothalamic cell populations, we performed RNAscope in situ hybridization for Tox3 combined with immunofluorescence labeling for neuronal nuclei antigen (NeuN, neuronal marker), vimentin (tanycyte marker), glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP, astrocyte marker), and ionized calcium binding adaptor molecule 1 (IBA1, microglia marker). The results revealed that Tox3 expression was predominantly neuronal, with most Tox3-positive cells co-expressing NeuN (90.54%), and almost all (>95%) NeuN-positive cells showing Tox3 expression (Figure S1b, c). In contrast, minimal colocalization was observed between Tox3 and markers of tanycytes, astrocytes, or microglia (Figure S1d-f). Consistent with these findings, analysis of a published single-cell RNA-sequencing dataset of the mouse hypothalamus confirmed that Tox3 was abundantly expressed in neurons, with negligible expression in tanycytes, astrocytes and microglia (Fig. 1c, d). These findings establish that TOX3 is specifically and highly expressed in hypothalamic neurons.

Knockdown of TOX3 in hypothalamic neurons exacerbates diet-induced obesity and metabolic dysfunctions
Given the prominent hypothalamic expression of TOX3, we examined its expression under different metabolic conditions. Hypothalamic Tox3 mRNA levels were significantly downregulated in high fat diet (HFD)-induced obese mice compared with chow diet (CD)-fed controls (Fig. 1e). To investigate the role of hypothalamic neuronal TOX3 in energy homeostasis, we bilaterally injected HFD-fed mice with AAV-shCtrl or AAV-shTox3 viruses (tracked with GFP) (Fig. 1f). Fluorescence imaging confirmed GFP expression in hypothalamic nuclei (ARC, VMH, DMH, LH, and PVN), with no detectable signal in extrahypothalamic regions such as the cortex (Fig. 1g). AAV-shTox3 injection significantly reduced hypothalamic Tox3 expression without affecting other family members (Tox, Tox2, Tox4) (Fig. 1h), while Tox3 levels remained unchanged in other regions including the thalamus, hippocampus and cortex (Figure S1g).

Hypothalamic Tox3 knockdown led to greater body weight gain (Fig. 1i; Figure S1h). Post-mortem analyses revealed increased weights of liver, epididymal WAT (eWAT), inguinal WAT (iWAT), and BAT (Fig. 1j), along with enlarged adipocytes in these depots (Fig. 1k-m). Livers of AAV-shTox3-injected mice exhibited more and larger lipid droplets (Fig. 1k) and elevated levels of hepatic triglycerides (TG), total cholesterol (TC), and non-esterified fatty acid (NEFA) (Fig. 1n-p). Compared with controls, mice with TOX3 knockdown in hypothalamic neurons displayed impaired glucose tolerance and reduced insulin sensitivity (Fig. 1q-t), accompanied by significantly higher serum insulin levels (Fig. 1u). Collectively, these results demonstrate that specific knockdown of TOX3 in hypothalamic neurons exacerbates HFD-induced obesity and metabolic dysfunction in mice.

Ablation of TOX3 in POMC-lineage cells exacerbates diet-induced obesity and metabolic disturbance
Hypothalamic POMC neurons is known as crucial nodes in energy homeostasis6,8,20. To determine TOX3 expression in these neurons, we generated POMC-lineage cell-specific tdTomato reporter mice (Pomc-cre;Ai9) and observed substantial co-localization of Tox3 mRNA with tdTomato-labeled POMC-lineage cells (Figure S2a). Interestingly, after 16 weeks of HFD feeding, Tox3 expression in POMC (tdTomato+)-lineage cells was significantly reduced compared to CD-fed controls (Figure S2a, b). A modest decrease in Tox3 expression was also observed in non-POMC (tdTomato-) cells (Figure S2c).

To investigate TOX3 function specifically in POMC-lineage cells, we generated POMC-lineage cell-specific TOX3 knockout mice (PTKO) by crossing Tox3flox/flox (LoxP) mice with Pomc-Cre mice (Figure S2d, e). These mice further crossed with tdTomato reporter mice to visualize POMC-lineage cells. RNAscope analysis confirmed efficient and specific deletion of Tox3 in POMC-lineage cells (Figure S2f-h), with no effect on their distribution or quantity (Figure S2i, j), indicating that Tox3 is not required for the development or survival of POMC-lineage cells.

We then performed a comprehensive metabolic phenotyping screen in mice fed a standard CD or HFD. Under CD, deletion of Tox3 in POMC-lineage cells impacted no detectable changes in body length, body weight or body weight gain, and body composition in male mice (Figure S3a-f). Serum TC, TG, NEFA, and glucose levels were also comparable (Figure S3g-j). Moreover, we did not observe any difference in glucose tolerance or insulin sensitivity between genotypes (Figure S3k, l). Similar results were observed in female mice fed a CD (Figure S3m-x).

In contrast, when challenged with HFD, male PTKO mice showed increased body weight gain without changes in body length (Fig. 2a-c; Figure S4a). Body composition analysis revealed elevated fat mass composition and reduced lean mass composition (Fig. 2d, e). PTKO males also exhibited increased weights of eWAT, iWAT, and BAT (Fig. 2f) and larger adipocytes in these depots (Fig. 2g-i). Consistent with increased adiposity, eWAT from PTKO mice showed upregulated expression of proinflammatory genes (Mcp1, Tnfα, F4/80, Cd68, Cd11b, Cd11c) (Figure S4b) and more F4/80-positive cells (Figure S4c, d), suggesting exacerbated adipose inflammation. In addition, liver weight was higher in PTKO mice (Fig. 2j), accompanied by larger liver size, greater lipid accumulation, and elevated hepatic TG, TC and NEFA (Fig. 2k-n). Serum TC was elevated, whereas TG and NEFA remained unchanged (Figure S4e-g). PTKO mice displayed impaired glucose tolerance and disrupted insulin sensitivity (Fig. 2o-r), together with higher serum insulin levels (Fig. 2s).

Similarly, when challenged with HFD, female PTKO mice exhibited increased body weight gain and fat mass composition, along with decreased lean mass composition (Figure S5a-e). Consistently, fat pads weights, including gonadal WAT (gWAT) and iWAT, were significantly increased in female PTKO mice (Figure S5f), with larger adipocyte sizes observed (Figure S5g-i). More lipid was accumulated in liver tissues of female PTKO mice (Figure S5j-n).

These data indicate that loss of Tox3 in POMC-lineage cells exacerbates diet-induced obesity and metabolic dysfunction in both sexes. Since knockout of TOX3 did not show gender differences, we selected male mice for subsequent experiments.

Overexpression of TOX3 in hypothalamic POMC-lineage cells mitigates HFD-induced metabolic dysfunction
Next, we evaluated whether gain-of-function TOX3 in hypothalamic POMC-lineage cells would be sufficient to ameliorate HFD-induced obesity and metabolic dysfunction. We generated POMC-lineage cell-specific TOX3-overexpressing mice (PTOE) via ARC injection of a Cre-dependent AAV (AAV-Tox3) into Pomc-Cre mice (Fig. 3a). Controls received AAV-GFP (Fig. 3a). Fluorescence imaging confirmed that GFP was specifically detected in the ARC, but not in other regions including the VMH, DMH, LH, cortex, and hippocampus (Figure S6a). We confirmed that hypothalamic Tox3 mRNA expression was upregulated in PTOE mice, while Tox, Tox2, and Tox4 were unaffected (Figure S6b). RNAscope analysis further confirmed that Tox3 was specifically overexpressed in POMC (tdTomato+)-lineage cells (Figure S6c).

On a chow diet, metabolic parameters were comparable between groups (Figure S6d-m). Under HFD challenge, mice with hypothalamic POMC-lineage cell-specific TOX3 overexpression exhibited significantly lower weight gain compared with their controls (Fig. 3b, c; Figure S6n). Body composition analysis revealed reduced fat weight, fat mass composition, and increased lean mass composition in PTOE mice (Fig. 3d, e). Post-mortem analyses also showed decreased weights of eWAT, iWAT, and BAT depots (Fig. 3f), along with smaller adipocyte sizes in eWAT and iWAT, as well as reduced lipid accumulation in BAT (Fig. 3g-i). Inflammatory infiltration in eWAT was ameliorated, as reflected by lower mRNA levels of Mcp1, F4/80, Cd68, and Cd11b (Figure S6o) and fewer F4/80-positive cells (Figure S6p). Additionally, PTOE mice exhibited significantly lower liver weight (Fig. 3j), accompanied by decreased lipid droplet accumulation (Fig. 3k) and reduced hepatic levels of TG, TC, and NEFA (Fig. 3l-n), indicating amelioration of hepatic steatosis. Serum TC levels were reduced in PTOE mice, while TG and NEFA remained unchanged (Figure S6q-s). Overexpression of TOX3 in POMC-lineage cells also improved glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity (Fig. 3o-r), consistent with lower serum insulin levels (Fig. 3s).

Together, these findings demonstrate that specific overexpression of TOX3 in POMC-lineage cells is sufficient to ameliorate obesity and metabolic disturbances in mice fed an HFD.

TOX3 in POMC-lineage cells controls energy expenditure and adipose tissue catabolism
To understand the underlying mechanisms of how TOX3 in POMC-lineage cells affects energy homeostasis, we conducted indirect calorimetry to assess metabolic parameters in both TOX3 loss- and gain-of-function mice upon HFD feeding. In male LoxP and PTKO mice, food and water intake did not differ significantly (Figure S7a, b). Instead, TOX3 deletion in POMC-lineage cells significantly decreased O2 consumption, CO2 production, and energy expenditure (Fig. 4a, b; Figure S7c-f), without alterations in the respiratory exchange ratio (RER) or physical activity (Figure S7g, h). These results were accompanied by decreased rectal temperature in PTKO mice (Fig. 4c). Notably, thermal images in the interscapular regions indicated that the temperature around BAT regions was markedly reduced upon TOX3 ablation (Fig. 4d, e). Given that adipose tissue is a well-known organ in energy expenditure and obesity progression, we further conducted thorough studies to examine catabolic metabolism in both BAT and WAT. TOX3 deletion markedly downregulated BAT thermogenic genes (Ucp1, Pgc1α, Dio2, Cidea) (Fig. 4f), while browning-related transcripts in iWAT were unaltered (Figure S7i). Western blot analysis and immunohistochemistry further confirmed significantly lower UCP1 protein in BAT of PTKO mice (Fig. 4g-i). The thermogenesis in BAT utilizes fatty acids derived from white adipose lipolysis21,22. Coordinately, we found the expression or phosphorylation of lipolytic proteins were significantly lower in eWAT and iWAT (Figure S7j-l). In liver, genes promoting fatty acid uptake (Cd36) and lipogenic (Srebf1) were upregulated, whereas genes involved in fatty acid oxidation (Cpt1α) and lipoprotein secretion (Apob, Mttp) were downregulated; meanwhile, skeletal muscle (SKM) metabolic markers remained unchanged (Figure S7m, n).

We next investigated whether TOX3 overexpression in POMC-lineage cells could enhance energy expenditure. In metabolic cage studies, food and water intake were unaltered between Control and PTOE groups (Figure S8a, b). However, PTOE mice exhibited significantly higher O2 consumption, CO2 production, and energy expenditure (Fig. 4j, k; Figure S8c-f), with no change in RER or locomotor activity (Figure S8g, h). Rectal and interscapular temperatures were also elevated in PTOE mice (Fig. 4l-n). Expression of UCP1 and other thermogenic markers was increased in BAT (Fig. 4o-r), while iWAT browning markers were unaltered (Figure S8i). Correspondingly, the expression of phosphorylation of lipolytic proteins were greatly increased in WAT (Figure S8j-l). In liver, genes promoting fatty acid uptake (Cd36) and lipogenesis (Srebf1, Acaca) were downregulated, while fatty acid oxidation (Cpt2) was increased; metabolic genes in SKM remained unaffected (Figure S8m, n). These results indicate that TOX3 in POMC-lineage cells affects obesity and metabolic disturbances through its regulation of adipose tissue metabolism and energy expenditure.

TOX3 in POMC-lineage cells modulates adipose tissue metabolism through sympathetic nervous regulation
Adipose tissue receives direct sympathetic innervation, with SNS activity serving as a key regulator of adipose tissue metabolism23,24. To investigate whether TOX3 in POMC-lineage cells regulates energy homeostasis via the SNS pathway, we performed comprehensive analyses in both TOX3 loss- and gain-of-function models upon HFD feeding conditions.

In PTKO mice, tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) expression, a rate-limiting step enzyme required for catecholamine synthesis11,25, was significantly decreased in BAT (Fig. 5a-c; Figure S9a). Consistently, norepinephrine (NE) content was reduced in BAT, eWAT, and iWAT, but not in liver (Fig. 5d; Figure S9b). Adrenergic receptors (Adrβ1, Adrβ2, and Adrβ3) were downregulated in BAT but unchanged in WAT depots (Figure S9c-e). NE turnover in BAT, based on NE content before and after injection of α-methyl-para-tyrosine (AMPT), an inhibitor of TH26-29, was also lower in PTKO mice (Fig. 5e). In addition, the downstream effectors of the β3-adrenergic receptor signaling, phosphorylation of cAMP response element-binding protein (CREB) and p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK), were both downregulated in BAT of PTKO mice (Figure S9f).

Cold exposure (4℃) further revealed impaired thermoregulation in PTKO mice, which showed a more rapid decline in rectal and interscapular BAT temperature (Figure S9g, h). While body weight and adipose depot weights were unchanged at room temperature, cold-exposed PTKO mice showed higher weights of BAT, eWAT and iWAT (Figure S9i-l), along with attenuated cold-induced upregulation of UCP1 and TH (Figure S9m-q). To confirm SNS involvement, we administered the β3-adrenergic agonist CL316,24330-32 or saline to HFD-fed LoxP and PTKO mice (Fig. 5f). We found that PTKO-induced higher BAT weight, lower thermogenic gene expression, and more lipid droplets were all abrogated by CL316,243 treatment (Fig. 5g-k).

Conversely, PTOE mice showed elevated TH expression in BAT (Fig. 5l-n; Figure S10a) and increased NE content in BAT, eWAT, and iWAT (Fig. 5o; Figure S10b). Adrenergic receptors (Adrβ2 and Adrβ3) were upregulated in BAT but not in WAT (Figure S10c-e). NE turnover and phosphorylation of CREB and p38 MAPK were also enhanced in BAT of PTOE mice (Fig. 5p; Figure S10f). To further confirm SNS involvement, we performed bilateral microinjections of 6-hydroxydopamine hydrobromide (6-OHDA), a selective catecholaminergic neurotoxin26,33, into the BAT pads of HFD-fed Control and PTOE mice (Fig. 5q; Figure S10g-i). Four weeks post-injection, the decreases in body weight and BAT weight observed in PTOE mice with an intact SNS were largely reversed (Fig. 5r; Figure S10j), with comparable expression of thermogenic parameters and BAT morphology between groups (Fig. 5s-v). We also performed bilateral injections of 6-OHDA into both the eWAT and iWAT depots of HFD-fed Control and PTOE mice (Figure S10k-m). Interestingly, this intervention did not alter the observed reduction in body weight and fat mass composition, or the increase in fat mass composition, in PTOE mice (Figure S10n, o). These findings demonstrate that TOX3 in POMC-lineage cells regulate energy expenditure through β-adrenergic signaling in BAT.

TOX3 controls the function of hypothalamic POMC-lineage cells
To provide insight into the central mechanisms through which TOX3 in POMC-lineage cells regulates system metabolism, we assessed whether TOX3 participates in the control of POMC-lineage cellular activity. HFD-fed Pomc-cre;Ai9 and PTKO;Ai9 mice were used for whole-cell current-clamp recordings (Fig. 6a). We observed that POMC-lineage cells in PTKO;Ai9 mice exhibited a significant decrease in spontaneous firing rate compared to those in Pomc-cre;Ai9 mice, along with a trend toward reduced membrane potential (Fig. 6b-d). Consistent with these electrophysiological findings, immunostaining revealed a significant reduction in c-FOS-positive POMC-lineage cells in PTKO;Ai9 mice (Fig. 6e, f). Furthermore, hypothalamic POMC expression was significantly reduced in PTKO mice at both mRNA (Fig. 6g) and protein levels (Fig. 6h, i) compared to LoxP controls, while other neuropeptides (Cart, Agrp, and Npy) remained unchanged (Fig. 6g). Conversely, TOX3 overexpression in POMC-lineage cells increased c-FOS immunoreactivity (Fig. 6j, k) and upregulated hypothalamic POMC expression (Fig. 6l-n), without altering Cart, Agrp, or Npy levels (Fig. 6l). These data establish TOX3 as a regulator of POMC-lineage cellular activity and peptide expression, revealing its essential role in maintaining the function of POMC-lineage cells within the hypothalamus.

TOX3 modulates AKT signaling by regulating PTEN degradation
To elucidate how TOX3 affects the function of POMC-lineage cells, we performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) on hypothalamus of LoxP and PTKO mice (Figure S11a). Based on gene expression of specific markers34, we classified the cells into 9 distinct clusters (Fig. 7a; Figure S11b, c). The proportion of cells in each cluster did not differ significantly between groups (Figure S11d). Neurons were further subclustered into 26 subsets, including POMC neurons (Fig. 7b; Figure S11e). Transcriptome analysis identified differentially expressed genes in POMC neurons of PTKO versus LoxP mice (Fig. 7c). KEGG enrichment analysis showed enrichment of these genes in nervous system-related pathways, including insulin signaling (Fig. 7d). We also conducted RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) on fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS)-sorted POMC-lineage cells from HFD-fed Pomc-cre;Ai9 and PTKO;Ai9 mice (Figure S12a). This analysis identified 448 upregulated and 647 downregulated transcripts in TOX3-deficient POMC-lineage cells (Figure S12b). Notably, KEGG analysis also highlighted enrichment in the Phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase (PI3K)-AKT signaling pathway (Figure S12c).

We further performed insulin administration experiments to confirm the involvement of TOX3 in insulin responses. As expected, while insulin robustly induced p-AKT (S473) expression in Pomc-cre;Ai9 mice, this effect was markedly attenuated in PTKO;Ai9 mice (Fig. 7e). In vitro, Tox3 knockdown attenuated insulin-induced p-AKT (S473) expression (Fig. 7f), whereas TOX3 overexpression enhanced this signaling (Fig. 7g; Figure S12d).

To elucidate how TOX3 influences insulin signaling, we performed immunoprecipitation-mass spectrometry (IP-MS) on hypothalamic lysates from mice injected with AAV-Tox3-Flag. PTEN, a key phosphatase in the insulin pathway, was identified as a potential TOX3-interacting partner (Fig. 7h). We further confirmed this interaction by additional Co-IP and western blot analyses (Fig. 7i). Immunofluorescence staining also revealed the co-localization of PTEN and TOX3 in N2a cells (Figure S12e). TOX3 manipulation did not alter Pten mRNA levels (Figure S12f, g). However, TOX3 overexpression significantly decreased PTEN protein levels both in vivo (Fig. 7j; Figure S12h) and in vitro (Fig. 7i), suggesting post-translational regulation. Cycloheximide (CHX) chase assays in GT1-7 and N2a cells showed that TOX3 overexpression significantly accelerated PTEN degradation (Fig. 7k, l; Figure S12j, k). Moreover, the proteasome inhibitor MG132 blocked the TOX3-mediated decrease in PTEN protein (Fig. 7m), suggesting that TOX3 promotes proteasome-dependent PTEN turnover. Furthermore, restoring PTEN expression in TOX3-overexpressing cells suppressed insulin-induced AKT phosphorylation at Ser473 (Fig. 7n; Figure S12l). These results demonstrate that TOX3 potentiates AKT signaling through post-translational suppression of PTEN.

TOX3 in hypothalamic AgRP neurons is dispensable for energy homeostasis
AgRP neurons in the ARC represent another key population involved in metabolic regulation35,36. We therefore investigated whether TOX3 in AgRP neurons contributes to whole-body metabolism regulation. First, we characterized TOX3 expression in AgRP neurons under different conditions. In situ hybridization confirmed Tox3 expression in AgRP neurons (Figure S13a), though at markedly lower levels compared to POMC-lineage cells (Figure S2a). Tox3 expression was slightly decreased in AgRP neurons of diet-induced obese mice relative to chow-fed controls (Figure S13a, b).

To assess TOX3 function, we generated AgRP-specific knockout mice (ATKO) by crossing LoxP mice with Agrp-Cre mice (ATKO), which yielded efficient and specific deletion (Figure S13c, d). When fed a standard CD, no differences were observed in body length, body weight gain, body composition, adipose mass weights, glucose tolerance, or insulin sensitivity in male (Figure S13e-l) and female (data not shown) LoxP and ATKO mice. Similar results were observed in HFD-fed males (Figure S14a-n) and females (data not shown). Additionally, no changes in metabolic parameters were detected in mice challenged with chronic HFD feeding (Figure S14o-v).

We next overexpressed TOX3 in AgRP neurons by bilaterally injecting AAV-Tox3 or AAV-GFP into the ARC of HFD-fed male Agrp-Cre mice (Figure S15a). qPCR and in situ hybridization confirmed successful Tox3 overexpression (Figure S15b, c). Consistent with the knockout results, TOX3 overexpression in AgRP neurons did not affect body weight gain, body composition, adipose depot weights, adipocyte size, glucose tolerance, insulin sensitivity, or serum parameters (Figure S15d-m). Moreover, no significant differences in metabolic cage parameters were observed between ATOE and control mice (Figure S15n-u). Collectively, these data demonstrate that TOX3 in AgRP neurons is dispensable for whole-body energy homeostasis.
