## Methods

Mice
Pomc-Cre and Agrp-Cre strains were obtained from the Jackson Laboratory (BarHarbor, ME, USA). Tox3flox/flox mice were kindly provided by Prof. Tao Huang at Shandong University. To generate cell type-specific Tox3 knockout mice, Tox3flox/flox mice were crossed with Pomc-Cre or Agrp-Cre mice to selectively delete Tox3 from POMC-lineage cells or AgRP neurons, respectively. The resulting mice are hereafter referred to as PTKO (POMC-lineage cell-specific TOX3 knockout) or ATKO (AgRP neuron-specific TOX3 knockout) mice, with Tox3 flox/flox mice (designated as LoxP controls) serving as controls.

To assess TOX3 expression in hypothalamic POMC-lineage cells and AgRP neurons, we crossed Pomc-Cre or Agrp-Cre mice with Rosa26-lox-stop-lox-tdTomato (Ai9) reporter mice (The Jackson Laboratory) to generate Pomc-cre;Ai9 or Agrp-cre;Ai9 mice, respectively, in which POMC- or AgRP-expressing cells were labelled with tdTomato. To confirm TOX3 deletion specifically in POMC-lineage cells, Pomc-Cre and PTKO mice were crossed with Ai9 mice to generate conditional knockout mice or control mice with POMC-lineage cells were labelled by tdTomato, hereafter referred to as Pomc-cre;Ai9 or PTKO;Ai9 mice, respectively. Similarly, to confirm TOX3 deletion specifically in AgRP neurons, Agrp-Cre and ATKO mice were crossed with Ai9 mice to generate conditional knockout mice or control mice with AgRP neurons were labelled by tdTomato, hereafter referred to as Agrp-cre;Ai9 or ATKO;Ai9 mice, respectively.

The animals were housed under a 12 h light/12 h dark cycle (lights on at 7:00 am, lights off at 7:00 pm) in a temperature-controlled room (22-24℃) and had ad libitum access to food and water unless otherwise indicated. Standard environmental enrichment was provided. Mice were fed a standard chow diet (CD) (52 g/kg fat, cd-dossy, Chengdu, Sichuan, China) or a high-fat diet (HFD) (60% kcal from fat, D12492, Research Diets, NJ, USA). Weekly body weight measurements were taken between 6 to 20 weeks of age. All surgical and tissue collection were performed during the light phase. All animal procedures were reviewed and approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Sichuan University (No: 20230731003).

Stereotaxic surgery
For hypothalamic neuron-specific TOX3 knockdown, we constructed neuronal-targeted AAV-hSyn-eGFP-miR30shRNA vectors targeting Tox3 (AAV-shTox3) or control (AAV-shCtrl). The miR30 backbone enhances shRNA processing and stability, promoting more potent and durable gene silencing compared to conventional shRNA designs52. For TOX3 overexpression in hypothalamic neurons, we constructed neuronal-targeted AAV-hSyn-eGFP-Flag vectors targeting Tox3 (AAV-Tox3-Flag) or control (AAV-GFP-Flag). These viruses were packaged by the ObiO Technology (Shanghai, China). To induce the specific knockdown or overexpression of TOX3 in hypothalamic neurons, wild-type (WT) C57BL/6J mice were anesthetized with isoflurane and then subjected to bilateral stereotaxic injections of AAV-shTox3/AAV-shCtrl (for knockdown), or AAV-GFP-Flag/AAV-Tox3-Flag (for overexpression) into the hypothalamus (coordinates: bregma, anterior-posterior, -1.5 mm; dorsal-ventral, -5.6 mm; lateral, ± 0.35 mm; 1000 nl per site).

To generate mouse models of Tox3 overexpression specifically in POMC-lineage cells or AgRP neurons, AAV-DIO-eGFP (AAV-GFP) and AAV-DIO-Tox3-eGFP (AAV-Tox3) vectors were generated, which were also packaged by ObiO Technology. To evaluate the therapeutic potential of TOX3 in the context of established obesity, Pomc-Cre or Agrp-Cre mice were first fed HFD for 8 weeks to induce obesity, and then anesthetized with isoflurane and received bilateral stereotaxic injections of either AAV-GFP or AAV-Tox3 vectors into the ARC (coordinates: bregma, anterior-posterior, -1.5 mm; dorsal-ventral, -5.85 mm; lateral, ± 0.3 mm; 500 nl per site).

Body length and composition analysis
The body length (nose-to-anus length) of mice was determined by measuring the linear distance from the rostral tip of the nose to the caudal base of the tail53. Body composition (lean and fat mass) was quantitatively assessed using the Small Animal Body Composition Analysis and Imaging System (MesoQMR23-060H-I; Nuimag Corp., Shanghai, China) at specified time points.

Metabolic cage measurements
Metabolic parameters, including food intake, water intake, oxygen consumption (VO2), carbon dioxide production (VCO2), energy expenditure, RER, and locomotor activity, were measured using the Promethion Metabolic Monitoring System (Sale Systems International, LV, USA). Following a 2-day acclimation period, continuous measurements were recorded over 72 h. Data are presented as both hourly values over the 72 h-period and as averaged values across the light (07:00-19:00) and dark phases (19:00-07:00).

Body temperature measurements in mice
Core body temperature was assessed via rectal measurement using a digital thermometer equipped with a specialized rectal probe (KEW, Nanjing, China), as previously described27. Interscapular BAT surface temperature was determined by standardized infrared imaging technique using a calibrated infrared thermal imaging camera (FORTRIC, Shanghai, China), as previously described27.

Glucose tolerance test (GTT) and insulin tolerance test (ITT)
For the GTT, mice were fasted for 6 h before receiving an intraperitoneal (i.p) injection of glucose dissolved in saline (2 g/kg body weight for CD-fed mice; 1 g/kg for HFD-fed mice). For the ITT, mice were fasted for 4 h prior to i.p. administration of insulin (0.75 U/kg for CD-fed mice; 1.5 U/kg for HFD-fed mice). Blood glucose levels were measured from the tail vein using an automatic glucose monitor (Accu-Check; Roche, Switzerland) at baseline (0 min) and at 15, 30, 60, 90, 120 min post-injection.

Biochemical and hormone analysis in the serum and liver
Blood samples were collected from mice, and serum was isolated by centrifugation at 6,000 g for 10 min. For hepatic biochemical analysis, liver samples were homogenized in phosphate buffer solution (PBS) and extracted using chloroform: methanol (2:1, v/v), followed by centrifugation at 3,000 g for 10 min. The following commercial assay kits were used for biochemical and hormonal measurements: glucose, TC, and TG (Biosino, Beijing, China); NEFA (LabAssay NEFA, Wako Chemicals, VA, USA); insulin (ELISA kit #10-1247-01, Mercodia, Sweden).

Norepinephrine turnover measurement
NE turnover was assessed using the AMPT method, as previously described26,27. Briefly, one cohort of mice was left untreated and sacrificed to obtain baseline tissue NE content. The remaining paired mice were injected with AMPT (300 mg/kg) at baseline, followed by a supplemental dose (150 mg/kg) 2 h later to sustain TH inhibition. Four hours after the initial AMPT injection, these mice were sacrificed, and adipose tissues were rapidly dissected, weighed, snap frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at -80℃ until analysis. NE content in adipose tissues was quantified according to an established protocol54. Briefly, tissues were homogenized in ice-cold extraction buffer (0.05 M hydrochloric acid in methanol) using a tissue dismembrator, followed by centrifugation at 12,000 g for 10 min at 4℃. The supernatant was collected, and 30 μL of tissue extract was mixed with 270 μL of 50% acetonitrile (in water) containing 0.05% ascorbic acid. After vortexing, the mixture was centrifuged again. Finally, 200 μL of the supernatant was analyzed by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) (AB6500, AB SCIEX, USA). NE turnover was calculated according to the following formulas: k = (lg[NE]0 -lg[NE]4)/(0.434 × 4) and K = k[NE]0, where k represents the rate constant of NE efflux, [NE]0 is the initial NE concentration, [NE]4 is the NE concentration after 4 hours, and K corresponds to NE turnover.

Activation and denervation of sympathetic nervous system activity
For acute cold exposure experiments, 16-week-old chow-fed mice were exposed to 4℃ for 6 h under fasting conditions. Rectal and interscapular BAT temperatures were monitored at specified time points, and tissues were collected after 6 hours of cold exposure for further analysis.

For the activation of sympathetic nervous system activity, 14-week-old HFD-fed mice were fasted for 2 h before and after an i.p. bolus injection of CL316,243 (1 mg/kg body weight) administered at 10:00 am to minimize confounding effects of feeding. Tissues were collected 4 h post-injection for further analysis.

For the sympathetic denervation in BAT or WAT, HFD-fed Pomc-Cre mice first received bilateral stereotaxic injections of either AAV-GFP or AAV-Tox3. Subsequently, local denervation was performed by injecting 6-OHDA (10 mg/mL in saline containing ascorbic acid) into the adipose depots. As previously described33,55, 6-OHDA was administered at five distinct sites per BAT pat, or at 15 distinct sites per eWAT and iWAT pad (1 μL per site). Adipose tissues were collected four weeks after chemical denervation for subsequent analysis.

Histological analysis
Mice were euthanized by CO2 inhalation prior to tissue collection. Tissues including liver, eWAT, iWAT, and BAT were collected and fixed in 10% PBS neutral buffered formalin (NBF) for 48-72. Following fixation, the samples were dehydrated and embedded in paraffin according to a standard procedure and sectioned into 4-μm sections for further use. For hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, tissue sections were processed according to the manufacturer’s protocol. For immunohistochemistry (IHC) analysis, antigen retrieval was performed using citrate acid buffer, followed by blocking with 10% normal donkey or goat serum for 1 h at room temperature. Primary antibodies were applied and incubated overnight at 4℃, followed by appropriate secondary antibody incubation for 1 h at room temperature. Signal detection was achieved using chromogenic substrates. Lipid accumulation was assessed in liver cryosections (8 μm) using Oil Red O staining according to established protocols. The sections were visualized under optics microscope (Olympus, Japan) or laser scanning confocal microscopy (Nikon, Japan). Quantitative analysis of IHC staining was performed using ImageJ software (NIH, Bethesda, MD, USA).

Immunofluorescence and RNA fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH)
Mice were deeply anesthetized with isoflurane and transcardially perfused with saline followed by ice-cold 4% paraformaldehyde in PBS prior to brain collection. For brain immunofluorescence staining, mice were transcardially perfused with saline followed by ice-cold 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) in PBS. Brains were dissected and post-fixed in 4% PFA for 24 h at 4℃, dehydrated in a graded sucrose series (10%, 20%, and 30% in PBS), and sectioned at 14 μm thickness. Brain sections were dried at 60℃ for 30 min, fixed in cold NBF for 15 min, and dehydrated through an increasing gradient ethanol. The slices were treated with hydrogen peroxide, and boiled in co-detection retrieval reagent, followed by primary incubation at 4℃ overnight. Subsequently, they were incubated with appropriate secondary antibodies and counterstained with DAPI.

For combined RNA fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) and immunofluorescence staining, mouse brain sections were processed using the RNAscope Multiplex Fluorescent Reagent Kit v2 and RNA-Protein Co-detection Ancillary Kit (323181 and 323100-USM, ACD, CA, USA) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Briefly, the brain slices were incubated with primary antibodies at 4℃ overnight. The slices were then incubated with Protease Plus (40℃, 30 min) followed by hybridization with the target probe (40℃, 2 h) in a HybEZTM oven (ACD). Then, signal amplification was achieved using amplifiers AMP1-3 and visualized by TSA Vivid Fluorophore 650. After HRP blocker treatment, the slices were incubated with corresponding secondary antibodies. Sections were then counterstained with DAPI for 2 min at room temperature and mounted.

Images were obtained using laser scanning confocal microscopy (Nikon, Japan; Zeiss, Germany). Quantitative analysis was performed using ImageJ software (NIH). For quantitative assessment of overall signal intensity within a defined anatomical region, we first delineated the entire ARC as the region of interest (ROI) based on a reference atlas and DAPI staining. The fluorescent intensity within the ROI was measured for the specific channel using ImageJ. For co-localization analyses, we manually outlined the ARC as the ROI in each section, guided by DAPI staining and anatomical landmarks. Within this ROI, the tdTomato-positive or negative cells were identified using the corresponding fluorescence channel, and the mean fluorescence intensity of another signal was measured in each cell. The percentage of co-localized cells was calculated per animal and used for statistical analysis.

Electrophysiology
Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings of neurons from Pomc-cre;Ai9 and PTKO;Ai9 mice fed with HFD were performed. Briefly, mice were deeply anesthetized with isoflurane and then transcardially perfused with 95% O2 and 5% CO2 oxygenated ice-cold NMDG cutting solution comprising 93 mM NMDG, 93 mM HCl, 2.5 mM KCl, 1.2 mM NaH2PO4, 30 mM NaHCO3, 25 mM D-glucose, 20 mM HEPES, 5 mM Na-ascorbate, 2 mM thiourea, 3 mM Na-pyruvate, 10 mM MgSO4, and 0.5 mM CaCl2. The brain was quickly removed and immersed in ice-cold NMDG cutting solution. Coronal brain slices containing ARC (250 μm) were cut with a Leica VT1200s vibratome, recovered at 34 ℃ for 10-13 min in NMDG cutting solution, and then maintained at 25 ℃ in oxygenated artificial cerebrospinal fluid (ACSF) (126 mM NaCl, 2.5 mM KCl, 2 mM CaCl2, 2 mM MgCl2, 26 mM NaHCO3, 1.25 mM NaH2PO4, and 10 mM glucose) for 1 h until recordings. Slices were transferred to the recording chamber and perfused with oxygenated ACSF (~ 3 ml/min). Slices were visualized with infrared optics using an upright microscope equipped with a 40× water-immersion lens (Examiner. A1). Neurons from ARC were identified by their location and fluorescence. While-cell patch-clamp recording of action potential (AP) was obtained with a MultiClamp 700B amplifier, a Digidata 1440A analog-to-digital converter, and pClamp 10.2 software (Molecular Devices). Voltage traces were sampled at 10 kHz and filtered at 2 kHz. Recording pipettes were filled with a solution containing: 135 mM K-gluconate, 5 mM KCl, 0.5 mM CaCl2, 10 mM HEPES, 2 mM Mg-ATP, 0.1 mM GTP, 5 mM EGTA, 300 mOsm). Resting membrane potentials (RMP) were measured within 1 min of break-in to the whole-cell configuration.

Single-nucleus RNA sequencing and data processing
For single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq), hypothalamic tissues were rapidly dissected from HFD-fed LoxP and PTKO mice immediately after euthanasia by CO2 inhalation, flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at -80℃ until processing. All subsequent snRNA-seq procedures were performed by Shanghai Applied Protein Technology Co., Ltd. Briefly, frozen tissues were thawed in lysis buffer and nuclei were isolated via gentle mechanic homogenization, followed by filtration and purification through a density gradient. Nuclei were resuspended in appropriate buffer, and their concentration was adjusted to approximately 1000 nuclei/μL. The suspension was then loaded onto the 10× Genomics Chromium Single Nuclei Gene Expression platform for library preparation and sequencing. Post-sequencing, FASTQ files were processed using CellRanger (10× Genomics) to generate raw count matrices by mapping RNAs to the transcriptome, assigning transcripts to individual cells, and removing duplicate reads. The resulting count matrices were processed using the Seurat package in R. Cell clusters were annotated based on canonical marker genes, which were cross-validated using CellMarkers 4.0 to ensure accurate cell-type identification.

Neuron isolation, fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS), and RNA sequencing
Hypothalamus from three Pomc-cre;Ai9 or PTKO;Ai9 male mice fed an HFD for 16 weeks were pooled per experimental sample. Single-cell suspensions were prepared using the Adult Brain Dissociation Kit (Miltenyi Biotec, #130-107-677) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, freshly dissected hypothalamus was rinsed in ice-cold Dulbecco’s PBS (D-PBS) and subsequently transferred into gentleMACS C Tubes (Miltenyi Biotec, #130-093-237) containing the enzymatic digestion mixture. Tissue dissociation was performed using the gentleMACS Octo Dissociator with Heaters (Miltenyi Biotec, #130-096-427). The resulting cell suspension was filtered through a 70 μm nylon mesh and centrifuged at 300 × g for 10 minutes at 4°C, followed by removal of cellular debris and erythrocytes. The pelleted cells were resuspended in D-PBS, and cell viability was assessed using 7-aminoactinomycin D (7-AAD; Beyotime Biotechnology, #C1053S, Shanghai, China). Fluorescence-activated cell sorting was conducted using a BD FACSAria SORP cell sorter (BD Biosciences) at the Flow Cytometry Core Facility. tdTomato-positive cells were selectively collected for subsequent RNA sequencing analysis, which was performed by Shi-Bio Technology (Wuhan, China).

Immunoprecipitation-mass spectrometry (IP-MS) and Co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP)
To identify TOX3-interacting partners in hypothalamic neurons, we generated a mouse model enabling neuro-specific overexpression of TOX3 within the hypothalamus. Four weeks post-injection, mice were euthanized by CO2 inhalation, and hypothalamic tissues were immediately isolated and homogenized in IP lysis buffer. Lysates were incubated with anti-Flag antibody overnight at 4°C, followed by incubation with Protein A/G magnetic beads (Selleck, #B23202) for 4 h at 4°C. After extensive washing with lysis buffer, immunoprecipitates were resolved by SDS-PAGE. Gel sections were excised for in-gel tryptic digestion, and resulting peptides were analyzed by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). Potential TOX3 interactors were defined as proteins exclusively identified in AAV-Tox3-Flag samples but absent in AAV-Flag controls.

For Co-IP validation, hypothalamic lysates from AAV-Tox3-Flag-injected mice were immunoprecipitated with either control IgG or anti-Flag antibody overnight at 4°C, followed by Protein A/G bead capture (4 h, 4°C). After washing, complexes were eluted and analyzed by SDS-PAGE and immunoblotting.

Cell culture, transfections, and treatments
GT1-7 cells and N2a cells were kindly provided by Prof. Lu Gan at Sichuan University. These cells were cultured in Dulbecco's Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and 1% penicillin/streptomycin at 37°C in a 5% CO₂ humidified atmosphere. To overexpress PTEN, the full-length coding sequence of mouse Pten was cloned into the pcDNA3.1-Myc vector, and cells were transfected with either Pten-Myc construct or empty vector control using LEPI transfection reagent. For TOX3 overexpression experiments, cells were transfected with vectors encoding either mouse Tox3-Flag or vehicle for 48 h. For TOX3 knockdown, cells were transfected with Tox3-specific small interfering RNA (siRNA) using Hiperfect transfection reagent (Qiagen, #301707) according to the manufacturer's protocol. For insulin signaling analysis, cells were serum-starved for 4 hours prior to stimulation with insulin (100 nM) for 0, 5, or 10 minutes at 37°C.

RNA extraction, reverse transcription, and quantitative PCR
Total RNA was extracted from tissues harvested from mice euthanized by CO2 inhalation using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. RNA quality was assessed by measuring the A260/A280 ratio using a NanoDrop 2000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). cDNA was generated by using a reverse transcription kit (Takara Bio, China) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Quantitative real-time (qPCR) was performed using a Real-Time PCR Detection System (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA, USA) with SYBR Green qPCR Master Mix (Vazyme, Nanjing, China). Target gene expression was normalized to 18s rRNA, and the results were presented as fold change by comparison with the control groups. All primer sequences are provided in Table S1.

Protein extraction and Western blot analysis
Tissue samples harvested from mice euthanized by CO2 inhalation or cell samples were homogenized in lysis buffer. The lysates were centrifuged at 12,000 g for 10 min at 4 °C to obtain clarified supernatants. Protein concentrations were determined using a bicinchoninic acid (BCA) protein assay kit (Sangon Biotech, Shanghai, China) following the manufacturer’s protocol. Equal amounts of proteins were loaded on SDS-PAGE gels, transferred to a nitrocellulose membrane, and probed with primary antibodies at 4℃ overnight. The following day, blots were rinsed and incubated with corresponding secondary antibodies for 1 h at room temperature, then visualized using the LI-COR Odyssey System (Lincoln, NE, USA). β-Actin served as the loading control for normalization. All primary antibodies used are detailed in Table S2. The uncropped blots were provided in the Source Data file.

Statistics
All statistical analyses were conducted using GraphPad Prism 9 software (GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA, USA). Data are expressed as mean ± SEM. Significance was determined by two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Sidak’s multiple comparisons test, unpaired two-tailed Student’s t test, and one-way ANOVA with post-hoc Tukey’s test as specified in the figure legends. Differences in the relationship between energy expenditure and lean body mass were analyzed by two-sided analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) with lean body mass included as a covariate, using the online tool CalR2 (available at CalR2 (calrapp.org)). A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The specific sample sizes (n values) for each experimental group are provided in the corresponding figure legends, representing biological replicates (individual mice). At least three independent experiments were repeated with similar results.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

In this manuscript the authors have investigated the role of the transcriptional co-regulator TOX3 in the regulation of energy balance. The authors claim a critical role for TOX3 in this context by action through the hypothalamic POMC neurons. The work as it stands is fundamentally incremental and characterized by several pitfalls and limitations that reduce the enthusiasm of this reviewer for the manuscript.
1. the authors have used a genetic approach (POMC-Cre mice) where recombination and deletion of TOX3 will not only happen during development, but it will also not exclusive of POMC neurons in the ARC. POMC precursors in the ARC give rise to several other neuronal types, including AgRP and kisspeptin neurons (PMID: 35044906; PMID: 20348924). POMC is also expressed during development in extrahypothalamic brain structures affecting feeding behavior, such as the hippocampus and amygdala, and in adulthood expression is maintained in the brainstem and pituitary. Authors do not provide any evidence that the modifications they see in their model applies specifically to hypothalamic POMC neurons in adulthood. This lack of specificity for POMC neurons in the ARC is obvious by the images provided in supplementary Figure 2. Authors have GFP and tdtomato expression in basically all cells in the ARC. Authors need to be aware that POMC-Cre-ERT2 genetic model is available in the field.
2. Similarly for the overexpression of TOX3 in POMC neurons, the authors do not provide any evidence that this is specific to POMC neurons. The expression of GFP fluorescence in supplementary figure 6 (panels A and C, not POMC as wrongly reported in panel C) does not prove specificity for POMC neurons and again by looking at the distribution of the signal, this does not seem the typical distribution for POMC neurons.
3. Conceptually speaking, although it is interesting that TOX3 regulates PTEN and AKT, there is already ample evidence of the role of the insulin-signlaing pathways in the hypothalamic control of energy balance, as the authors also mention in the discussion.
4. In general, this reviewer finds the work an excellent phenotypic characterization of the animal models studied, but again, the effects observed concerning lipid and glucose metabolism are often the results of animals gaining more (in the KO) or less (in the overexpression model), and modulation of the sympathetic output (again not surprising).
5. This reviewer wonder if the POMC KO phenotype described is the result of altered cell proliferation/neurodevelopment (figure 6H, less POMC protein or less POMC neurons?) considering that TOX3 is removed from POMC cell precursors and that TOX3 has a role in neurodevelopment, as mentioned by the authors in their introduction.
6. Analysis of downregulation/overexpression of TOX3 by RNAscope is rather qualitative. Other quantitative methods should be included.
7. data in figure 1, what about expression of TOX 3 in other brain areas in addition to the hypothalamus? And in which part of the hypothalamus were the images shown in Fig. 1B taken from? In data shown in Fig. 1 G, authors should verify changes in TOX3 expressions in structure just above those receiving the injection, including thalamus and hippocampus. Are “WT” mice, C57Bl6 mice? Please provide correct information.
8. for all data with BW change (for example Fig. 1H, 2B, 3B…), authors need to provide actual BW curve and changes before/after AAV administration.
9. Concerning the snRNAseq data: in Suppl Figure 11C, by looking at the UMAP plots, it seems that there are differences in astrocytes, tanycytes and olygodendrocytes? Is it the case?
10. Data in cell lines: did authors check for expression of POMC in the cell lines used? GT1-7 cells do not express POMC, but are known model for GnRH neurons. Same for N2acells, they are known to not express POMC endogenously.
11. Statistical analyses: authors state they used one way ANOVA, but for several analysis they need to carry out either repeated ANOVAs (time is a factor, together with genotype) or 2 way ANOVAs (genotypes and diets or treatments as factors).
12. Are Tox3 flox mice characterized? Are there data showing the model works properly?
13. In general, for the representation of the data, authors should include SEM represented in both directions.
14. For indirect calorimetry data, authors should refrain from correcting the representation of the data by lean mass (Fig. 4A, 4J….) for the energy expenditure, as this representation would be misleading given diffreences in body weight of the animals studies.
15. For all western blot analyses throughout the manuscript, 3 samples/condition is too low and it does not reflect the biological variability that it is associated to these types of measurements.
16. In general, description of methods lacks details/information for several experiments shown in the figures. For instance, how is NE turnover carried out exactly ? How quantification of the different labelling in the hypothalamic images shown are carried out? What ROI was used? Details about the different surgeries carried out is missing. Details about the housing of the animals (single/grouped housing), when light is on/off, when experiments are done in relation to the light cycle, cages enrichment, info about chow diet used are missing. Line 537, why is a mir30 shRNA used? And later in the text, how were tissues collected/prepared/processed for snRNAseq?
17. Wording is awkward in several parts of the manuscript, for instance: line 53 “peripheral” activation- this is rather central activation of peripheral SNS output; line 55 “directly” -POMC neurons do not “directly” innervate the adipose tissue, that happens through multi-synaptic connections onto SNS neurons. Line 86, “POMC neuron-derived TOX3” odd phrasing, TOX3 is not produced/secreted by POMC neurons.
18. Clarify in all figure legends if data are from males (Figure 1? Figure 3?...) or females.

### Reviewer 2

While obesity and related metabolic disorders such as type 2 diabetes and fatty liver disease have become a growing public health concern, the molecular mechanisms controlling central energy balance remain incompletely understood. Previous studies established that the hypothalamus, particularly pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) neurons in the arcuate nucleus, a first-order metabolic sensor, serves as a central regulator of energy homeostasis. In this study, the authors identified thymocyte selection-associated high mobility group box 3 (TOX3) as a key transcriptional co-regulator in hypothalamic POMC neurons. By utilizing cell-type specific genetic mouse models, the authors demonstrated that conditional deletion of TOX3 in POMC neurons exacerbates high-fat diet (HFD)–induced obesity, adipocyte hypertrophy, hepatic steatosis, and insulin resistance, whereas TOX3 overexpression protects mice against these metabolic abnormalities. Indirect calorimetry and thermography results revealed that TOX3 enhanced adipose tissue metabolism and energy expenditure through stimulating sympathetic outflow to adipose tissue, promoting lipolysis and brown adipose thermogenesis. Mechanistically, they identified a novel regulatory effect of TOX3 in proteasomal degradation of PTEN, leading to enhanced AKT signaling and increased POMC neuronal activity. Meanwhile, similar manipulations in agouti-related peptide (AgRP) neurons showed no significant metabolic effects. Although TOX3 has been previously implicated in metabolic disorders, this study newly identifies hypothalamic TOX3, specifically within POMC neurons, as a key regulator of energy homeostasis. And this effect is mediated through the TOX3–PTEN–AKT signaling axis. The data are rather comprehensive. There are several issues the authors should address to improve the manuscript.
Specific comments:
1. The title of the manuscript is somewhat vague. It would be better if the authors would revise it and improve the clarity. A suggested title is “TOX3 in hypothalamic POMC neurons improves adipose tissue energy homeostasis by targeting PTEN–AKT signaling axis.”
2. The authors examined the TOX3 mRNA expression across various mouse tissues and cell types using qPCR and RNAscope. It would strengthen the study if they also verified TOX3 distribution using available single-cell RNA sequencing databases to confirm TOX3 distribution across tissues and neuronal cell types.
3. In addition to comparing TOX3 levels between chow diet–fed and high-fat diet–fed mice, the authors can incorporate analysis of relevant human datasets to enhance the clinical relevance. If the human datasets are not available, the limitation should be clearly discussed.
4. In Supplementary Figure 2A, most TOX3 signals appear to be located outside POMC neurons, and high-fat diet treatment does not seem to significantly reduce TOX3 expression, which seems to be inconsistent with the results shown in Figure 1D. The rationale of focusing on POMC neuron–specific TOX3 should be better elaborated.
5. The degree of obesity differs between the loss-of-function and gain-of-function experiments. The control group in the gain-of-function study (Control) appears more obese than the LoxP control group in the loss-of-function study, with higher body weight, liver weight, and more fat tissue. Please explain this inconsistency.
6. The study proposes that TOX3 in POMC neurons regulates adipose tissue metabolism through sympathetic nervous system modulation. In addition to assessing NE content and turnover, the authors should also examine the expression levels of β-adrenergic receptors in adipose tissues to support this mechanistic claim.
7. The study only confirms the protective role of the sympathetic nervous system in TOX3-mediated effects in brown adipose tissue (BAT) using 6-hydroxydopamine hydrobromide (6-OHDA). The authors should also evaluate the effects of sympathetic inhibition in white adipose tissue (WAT) before concluding that the protective effect is specifically mediated via BAT.
8. The current study focuses on the TOX3/POMC effect on the adipose tissue, but some of the adipose data were associations, meaning the author cannot exclude the effect of TOX3/POMC on extra-adipose tissues. The systemic use of β3-adrenergic agonist also has its limitation in interpreting the adipose phenotype. The authors should profile the expression of key metabolic genes in the liver and skeletal muscles to see if there are collateral benefits in these metabolically important extra-adipose tissues.

### Reviewer 3

The manuscript by Qin Tang, Juan Pang and Jinhang Zhang et al. presents a compelling and well-designed study that significantly advances the understanding of central regulation of energy homeostasis. The authors provide robust evidence identifying TOX3 as a critical and previously overlooked metabolic regulator specifically within POMC neurons. Using genetic models, the authors show that TOX3 loss exacerbates diet-induced obesity, while its overexpression improves metabolism via a post-translational mechanism involving PTEN degradation and enhanced AKT signaling. The findings reveal a neuron-specific role for TOX3 in energy homeostasis and suggest its potential as a therapeutic target for metabolic disorders. However, there are some experiments and descriptions need to be improved.
Major concerns:
1. The authors should discuss the apparent discrepancy wherein POMC neuron-specific TOX3 ablation shows no phenotype on a chow diet (CD), despite the significant metabolic effect observed upon broader hypothalamic TOX3 knockdown under the same conditions. Please clarify whether this suggests that TOX3 in non-POMC hypothalamic neurons is responsible for the metabolic regulation observed under CD, and how this aligns with the proposed POMC-specific role for TOX3.
2. It would also be important to know the phenotypic effects of overexpressing TOX3 in POMC neurons under chow diet conditions, to fully elucidate its physiological role without the confounder of dietary stress.
3. The authors should address the discrepancy between the increased energy expenditure and the unaffected RER in PTKO mice.
4. Given the reduced thermogenesis in BAT, were there also corresponding changes in the beiging markers of WAT?
5. Evidence demonstrating the efficacy of 6-OHDA-mediated sympathetic denervation (e.g., measurements of tissue norepinephrine levels or tyrosine hydroxylase staining) should be provided.
Minor concerns：
1. Regarding Figure 6J, it appears that the green fluorescence channel may be missing from the merged image. This should be clarified or corrected.
2. For the Tox3 in situ hybridization data validating the knockdown efficiency, it is recommended that representative images be provided that more accurately reflect the corresponding quantitative results.

## Authors' Response to Round 1

Dear Reviewers:
Thank you for your letter and for the reviewers’ comments concerning our manuscript
entitled “TOX3 controls energy homeostasis in hypothalamic POMC neurons” (ID:
NCOMMS-25-70758-T). These comments are all valuable and very helpful for
revising and improving our paper, as well as guiding our research. We have studied
the comments carefully and have made corrections, hoping they will meet with your
approval. The major modifications in the revised manuscript are tracked in red, and
our point-by-point responses to the reviewer’s comments are provided below:
Reviewer #1
In this manuscript the authors have investigated the role of the transcriptional
co-regulator TOX3 in the regulation of energy balance. The authors claim a critical
role for TOX3 in this context by action through the hypothalamic POMC neurons.
The work as it stands is fundamentally incremental and characterized by several
pitfalls and limitations that reduce the enthusiasm of this reviewer for the manuscript.
Response: Thank you for your thorough, constructive review and for the time
invested in evaluating our manuscript. We appreciate your central concern regarding
the specificity of our models and the conceptual novelty of the findings.
In response, we have conducted additional experiments, analyses, and revisions to
address each point directly. Below, we provide point-by-point responses and outline
the changes made in the revised manuscript.
1. The authors have used a genetic approach (POMC-Cre mice) where recombination
and deletion of TOX3 will not only happen during development, but it will also not
exclusive of POMC neurons in the ARC. POMC precursors in the ARC give rise to
several other neuronal types, including AgRP and kisspeptin neurons (PMID:
35044906; PMID: 20348924). POMC is also expressed during development in
extrahypothalamic brain structures affecting feeding behavior, such as the
hippocampus and amygdala, and in adulthood expression is maintained in the
brainstem and pituitary. Authors do not provide any evidence that the modifications
they see in their model applies specifically to hypothalamic POMC neurons in
adulthood. This lack of specificity for POMC neurons in the ARC is obvious by the
images provided in supplementary Figure 2. Authors have GFP and tdTomato
expression in basically all cells in the ARC. Authors need to be aware that
POMC-Cre-ERT2 genetic model is available in the field.
Response: Thank you for raising this critical point regarding the specificity of the
genetic model used in our study. We acknowledge that the constitutive POMC-Cre
driver can mediate recombination in POMC-derived lineages beyond mature ARC
POMC neurons, as well as in extrahypothalamic regions, which is an inherent
limitation of this widely used tool.
While the inducible POMC-Cre-ERT2 model would offer superior temporal control,
generating a new TOX3 conditional knockout on this background is not feasible
within the revision timeline. Instead, we respectfully highlight key experimental
evidence that collectively supports a primary role for TOX3 in adult hypothalamic
POMC neurons in regulating energy balance.
Most critically, we performed adult-onset, ARC POMC neurons-restricted
overexpression of TOX3 using stereotactic delivery of a Cre-dependent AAV
(AAV-DIO-Tox3) into POMC-Cre mice. This intervention produced a phenotype
functionally opposite to the constitutive knockout: while genetic Tox3 deletion
increased body weight and adiposity with reduced energy expenditure, adult-specific
TOX3 overexpression reduced body weight and adiposity while increasing energy
expenditure (see Figure 2-4 in our revised manuscript). Although contributions from
other Cre-expressing cells cannot be entirely excluded in our knockout model, the
concordance between the knockout phenotype and the adult ARC-specific
overexpression phenotype strongly prioritizes the hypothalamic POMC neuron
population as the primary site of action for the metabolic effects of TOX3.
Regarding the images in Supplementary Figure 2, the tdTomato signal is from the Ai9
reporter allele crossed into our models, which is a widely used tool to label POMC
neurons in the ARC in previous studies1, 2. The widespread labeling in the ARC is
consistent with the known behavior of this driver line. Importantly, these data confirm
a significant reduction of Tox3 mRNA specifically within the tdTomato+ cell
population in the ARC upon Cre-mediated recombination, validating effective
knockdown within our targeted lineage.
We have explicitly addressed this model limitation in the revised Discussion as
follows: Third, the constitutive Pomc-Cre driver used here may mediate
recombination beyond mature POMC neurons, including in extrahypothalamic
lineages and developmental precursors3, 4, complicating phenotypic attribution. While
our AAV-based approach achieved adult-onset overexpression, the loss-of-function
model still carries the possibility of contributions from Tox3 deletion in off-target cell
populations. The development and application of temporally controlled genetic tools
will be necessary to precisely define the adult-specific functions of Tox3 in POMC
neurons.
2. Similarly for the overexpression of TOX3 in POMC neurons, the authors do not
provide any evidence that this is specific to POMC neurons. The expression of GFP
fluorescence in supplementary figure 6 (panels A and C, not POMC as wrongly
reported in panel C) does not prove specificity for POMC neurons and again by
looking at the distribution of the signal, this does not seem the typical distribution for
POMC neurons.
Response: Thank you for raising this important point and for bringing the labeling
error in panel C to our attention. We regret any confusion it may have caused and
appreciate the opportunity to clarify our viral strategy and the controls for specificity.
First, we would like to emphasize that our approach was designed to achieve both
genetic and anatomical specificity. We used a Cre-dependent AAV (AAV-DIO-Tox3)
that expresses the transgene exclusively in the presence of Cre recombinase. This
virus was stereotactically delivered into the ARC region of adult POMC-Cre mice.
Therefore, TOX3 overexpression is genetically restricted to Cre-expressing cells
within the POMC lineage and spatially confined to the viral injection site in the ARC,
as supported by the localized GFP expression shown in our original Supplemental
Figure 6a (Figure R1.1a).
Regarding panel C, we apologize for the erroneous labeling in the original figure
legend. The green signal in this panel is not GFP but corresponds to tdTomato
immunofluorescence. In these experiments, we used Pomc-cre;Ai9 mice, in which all
Cre-expressing cells are genetically labelled with tdTomato. Because the RNAscope
procedure completely quenches endogenous tdTomato fluorescence, we performed
immunofluorescence for tdTomato along with RNAscope to visualize the targeted cell
population, as described in our Methods section. This panel thus shows the
co-localization of tdTomato-labeled POMC lineage cells (green) with virally
overexpressed Tox3 mRNA (red, detected by RNAscope), confirming successful
delivery and expression within the intended Cre-expressing population.
To further strengthen our evidence, we have replaced the original panel C with a
higher-magnification image that more clearly shows Tox3 mRNA localized within
tdTomato+ cells in the ARC region (Figure R1.1b). We have also carefully corrected
the figure legend to accurately describe the methodology and signals represented.

3. Conceptually speaking, although it is interesting that TOX3 regulates PTEN and
AKT, there is already ample evidence of the role of the insulin-signaling pathways in

Response: We thank the reviewer for this comment and appreciate the reviewer's
acknowledgment of the established role of insulin signaling in the hypothalamus for
regulating energy homeostasis. As noted in our discussion, our goal was not simply to
associate TOX3 with this canonical pathway, but to identify it as a novel upstream
regulator that specifically modulates a key node within this pathway in POMC
neurons.
While insulin is a primary activator of PI3K-AKT, the intrinsic mechanisms that set
the basal tone or sensitivity of this pathway in POMC neurons remain less understood.
Our study identifies TOX3 as a novel, neuron-enriched factor that critically regulates
this pathway through its effect on PTEN, a major negative regulator. Importantly, our
findings reveal a previously unreported mechanism whereby TOX3 influences PTEN
protein stability, adding a novel regulatory layer to this essential metabolic signaling
module. And this advances the field from knowing that the pathway is important to
understanding how its baseline activity is wired into the identity of these crucial
metabolic cells.
We have incorporated the following statements into the revised Discussion to more
clearly articulate this conceptual contribution: “Our findings significantly extend this
understanding by identifying TOX3 as a key upstream regulator of insulin signaling
cascades in POMC neurons.” “our study establishes a direct functional link between
TOX3-previously uncharacterized in hypothalamic function-and a core metabolic
signaling axis within the specific POMC neuronal population central to energy
homeostasis”. “Moreover, we have identified a novel molecular interaction between
TOX3 and PTEN that reveals a previously unrecognized mechanism of metabolic
regulation”.
4. In general, this reviewer finds the work an excellent phenotypic characterization of
the animal models studied, but again, the effects observed concerning lipid and
glucose metabolism are often the results of animals gaining more (in the KO) or
less (in the overexpression model), and modulation of the sympathetic output (again not

Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the positive assessment of our
phenotypic work and for raising these critical points.
(1) Regarding the possibility that glucose/lipid phenotypes are secondary body
weight/composition change.
We agree with the reviewer’s insightful perspective. The glucose intolerance in PTKO
mice and the improved tolerance in PTOE mice under high-fat diet (HFD) appear
tightly coupled to changes in adiposity. Notably, under chow diet (CD)-where body
weight remained comparable-we observed no significant differences in fasting
glucose or glucose/insulin tolerance (see our Figure S3j-l and Figure S6k-m). These
suggest that systemic glucose alterations are likely secondary to changes in body
weight and adiposity resulting from TOX3 manipulation in POMC neurons.
Nevertheless, even under CD without significant weight differences, we detected
changes in the expression of key hepatic lipid metabolism genes (Figure R1.2a,b).
This indicates that TOX3 in POMC neurons can influence hepatic lipid metabolic

pointing to a more direct effect on liver metabolism that warrants future investigation.
Most importantly, this careful phenotypic dissection underscores the central finding of
our study: TOX3 in POMC neurons plays a primary and potent role in determining
body weight and adiposity set point. The discovery of a novel key regulator that
robustly governs energy expenditure through the canonical
POMC→sympathetic→BAT axis represents a significant conceptual advance.

remain unanswered, including whether hypothalamic POMC neuron TOX3 directly

Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful and technically precise
comment regarding the cell lines used in our study.
The reviewer is correct that GT1-7 cells are primarily a model for GnRH neurons,
while N2a cells are a neuroblastoma line; neither is a canonical, high-fidelity model

of endogenous Pomc expression in both lines (Ct ~29 in GT1-7; Ct ~24 in N2a).
This reflects a broader technical limitation in the field of hypothalamic neurobiology:
well-characterized, faithful in vitro models of specific neuronal populations, such as
POMC neurons, remain scarce. In the absence of such ideal systems, established
neuronal cell lines have been employed in prior studies1, 9 to dissect molecular
mechanisms relevant to hypothalamic signaling pathways-including those central to
our investigation-providing a precedent for their use in this context.

mechanistic studies of the TOX3-PTEN-AKT axis in a neuronal setting. We have
added the following statements in the revised manuscript to explicitly acknowledge
this limitation: Furthermore, the lack of ideal cellular models that faithfully
recapitulate POMC neurons remains a limitation in the field. Although GT1-7 and
N2a cells have been used in prior studies1, 9 and in the present study as in vitro models
for POMC research, neither fully recapitulates the molecular profile of mature POMC
neurons. Future studies would benefit from developing more physiologically relevant
systems—such as POMC-enriched cell lines or hypothalamic organoids—to better
model cell-autonomous mechanisms in these neurons.

Reviewer #2
While obesity and related metabolic disorders such as type 2 diabetes and fatty liver
disease have become a growing public health concern, the molecular mechanisms
controlling central energy balance remain incompletely understood. Previous studies
established that the hypothalamus, particularly pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC)
neurons in the arcuate nucleus, a first-order metabolic sensor, serves as a central
regulator of energy homeostasis. In this study, the authors identified thymocyte
selection-associated high mobility group box 3 (TOX3) as a key transcriptional
co-regulator in hypothalamic POMC neurons. By utilizing cell-type specific genetic
mouse models, the authors demonstrated that conditional deletion of TOX3 in POMC
neurons exacerbates high-fat diet (HFD)–induced obesity, adipocyte hypertrophy,
hepatic steatosis, and insulin resistance, whereas TOX3 overexpression protects mice
against these metabolic abnormalities. Indirect calorimetry and thermography results
revealed that TOX3 enhanced adipose tissue metabolism and energy expenditure
through stimulating sympathetic outflow to adipose tissue, promoting lipolysis and
brown adipose thermogenesis. Mechanistically, they identified a novel regulatory
effect of TOX3 in proteasomal degradation of PTEN, leading to enhanced AKT
signaling and increased POMC neuronal activity. Meanwhile, similar manipulations
in agouti-related peptide (AgRP) neurons showed no significant metabolic effects.
Although TOX3 has been previously implicated in metabolic disorders, this study
newly identifies hypothalamic TOX3, specifically within POMC neurons, as a key
regulator of energy homeostasis. And this effect is mediated through the TOX3–
PTEN–AKT signaling axis. The data are rather comprehensive. There are several
issues the authors should address to improve the manuscript.
Response: We thank you for the positive assessment of our study on hypothalamic
TOX3 in energy homeostasis via POMC neurons. Your constructive feedback is
highly valuable. In response, we have conducted additional experiments, analyses,
and revisions to address each point directly. Below, we provide point-by-point
responses and outline the changes made in the revised manuscript.
Specific comments:
1. The title of the manuscript is somewhat vague. It would be better if the authors
would revise it and improve the clarity. A suggested title is “TOX3 in hypothalamic
POMC neurons improves adipose tissue energy homeostasis by targeting PTEN–AKT
signaling axis.”
Response: Thank you for the helpful suggestion to improve the manuscript title. In
response, we have revised the title to: “TOX3 in hypothalamic POMC neurons
regulates energy balance via the PTEN-AKT signaling axis” to accurately and
concisely captures a central mechanistic finding of our study. We believe this change
significantly enhances the clarity and focus of our manuscript, and we sincerely
appreciate this constructive recommendation.
2. The authors examined the TOX3 mRNA expression across various mouse tissues
and cell types using qPCR and RNAscope. It would strengthen the study if they also
verified TOX3 distribution using available single-cell RNA sequencing databases to
confirm TOX3 distribution across tissues and neuronal cell types.
Response: Thank you for this excellent suggestion. As suggested, we have analyzed
publicly available datasets.
First, examination of bulk RNA-seq data across tissues (PRJCA019393) confirmed
that Tox3 mRNA expression is significantly higher in the brain compared to peripheral
tissues (Figure R2.1a), consistent with our initial qPCR results (see Supplementary
Figure 1a). To achieve higher resolution, we then examined Tox3 expression across
different brain regions. This analysis revealed that Tox3 expression levels are highest
in the hypothalamus, being significantly higher than those in the thalamus,
hippocampus, and cortex (Figure R2.1b).
Most importantly, as suggested, we interrogated existing mouse hypothalamic
scRNA-seq datasets (GSE188646). These data robustly corroborated our RNAscope
findings, demonstrating that Tox3 expression is predominantly enriched in neuronal
populations, with minimal expressions in astrocytes, tanycytes, and microglia (Figure
R2.1c,d). An interesting additional observation was unexpectedly high Tox3
expression in oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) (Figure R2.1d), which hints at
a potential novel role for TOX3 in OPC biology, a point we have discussed in the
revised Discussion section.
We have integrated these new analyses into the revised manuscript, presenting them in
the Results section and as new Fig. 1a-d.

Response: We thank the reviewer for the valuable suggestion to enhance the clinical

were unable to identify human data that directly compare TOX3 expression in the
brain under different dietary conditions. We have therefore explicitly acknowledged
this as a current limitation in the Discussion section of the revised manuscript as
follows: Finally, while our murine models have provided mechanistic insights into
TOX3's role in POMC neurons, we note that direct evidence linking TOX3 expression
to obesity in humans is currently unavailable. Future studies that incorporate human
datasets or relevant physiological models, such as hypothalamic organoids derived
from human pluripotent stem cells, would help establish the translational relevance of
this pathway in human energy homeostasis.

Response: Thank you for your insightful comment.
To address the concern directly, we have replaced the original image in
Supplementary Figure 2A with a more representative one and performed new
quantitative analysis using ImageJ. This re-analysis specifically measured Tox3
mRNA fluorescence intensity within POMC (tdTomato-positive) neurons. The results
confirm a significant reduction in Tox3 signal in POMC neurons under high-fat diet
(HFD) compared to chow diet (CD) (Figure R2.2a,b).
We fully agree with the reviewer’s observation that Tox3 is also expressed in other
cell types within the ARC, as evidenced by signal in tdTomato-negative cells.
Quantitative analysis of these non-POMC cells indeed shows a modest, though less
pronounced, decrease under HFD (Figure R2.2c). This finding, together with the
whole-hypothalamus data in Figure 1D, supports that Tox3 expression is not exclusive
to POMC neurons but is more widespread in the hypothalamus. We acknowledge that
we cannot exclude a functional role for TOX3 in other neuronal populations or
regions.

Our decision to focus on POMC (and AgRP) neurons stems from several established
considerations: (1) our preliminary data showed that hypothalamic Tox3 knockdown
disrupts whole-body energy homeostasis; (2) the ARC is a key hypothalamic nucleus
for metabolic regulation; and (3) POMC and AgRP neurons represent the two primary,
antagonistic populations within the ARC that centrally coordinate energy balance12, 13,
14. Studying TOX3 in these well-defined, metabolically critical neurons provides a
clear and physiologically relevant model to dissect its cell-type-specific role.
We have incorporated the following statements in the Discussion section of our
revised manuscript: First, although we have comprehensively characterized TOX3
expression and function in POMC and AgRP neurons, it is also expressed in other
hypothalamic neuronal populations. Moreover, while minimal Tox3 expression was
detected in tanycytes, astrocytes, and microglia, public scRNA-seq datasets indicate
that Tox3 is enriched in oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs), suggesting a
potential role in glial biology. The physiological relevance of TOX3 in these other
neuronal and non-neuronal cell types, particularly under metabolic challenge,
represents an important avenue for future research.
5. The degree of obesity differs between the loss-of-function and gain-of-function
experiments. The control group in the gain-of-function study (Control) appears more
obese than the LoxP control group in the loss-of-function study, with higher body
weight, liver weight, and more fat tissue. Please explain this inconsistency.
Response: Thank you for raising this important observation regarding the baseline
adiposity differences between the control groups in our loss-of-function and
gain-of-function studies. We appreciate the opportunity to clarify this point.
The apparent discrepancy arises primarily from the distinct experimental designs,
especially the timing of high-fat diet (HFD) initiation relative to the intervention.
In the loss-of-function study, both LoxP and PTKO mice began HFD at 6 weeks of age
and remained on the diet for 12 weeks. In contrast, in the gain-of-function study,
Pomc-Cre mice underwent an 8-week HFD pre-feeding period to establish
obesity before AAV-mediated TOX3 overexpression (or control). After intervention,
they continued HFD for another 12 weeks. As a result, the control group in the
gain-of-function study had already accumulated 8 weeks of HFD-induced weight gain
prior to the experimental comparison, naturally leading to higher baseline adiposity,
liver weight, and body weight than the controls in the loss-of-function study.
Additionally, the two studies used independent cohorts of mice with different genetic
backgrounds (Tox3flox/flox controls vs. Pomc-Cre controls), bred and maintained at
different times. While diet and housing conditions were standardized, some
inter-cohort variability in the severity of diet-induced obesity is common and can
influence absolute metabolic parameters.
Thus, the difference in control phenotypes is not an inconsistency but a logical
outcome of the distinct experimental timelines and cohorts. The central and consistent
finding across both studies remains clear: reducing TOX3 exacerbates obesity, while
increasing it confers protection—each relative to its internally matched control group.
We have clarified these methodological details in the revised manuscript to ensure
transparency.
6. The study proposes that TOX3 in POMC neurons regulates adipose tissue
metabolism through sympathetic nervous system modulation. In addition to assessing
NE content and turnover, the authors should also examine the expression levels of
β-adrenergic receptors in adipose tissues to support this mechanistic claim.
Response: Thank you for raising this insightful suggestion, which prompted us to
strengthen our mechanistic analysis. As suggested, we have conducted qPCR analysis
to examine the mRNA expression levels of β-adrenergic receptors (Adrβ1, Adrβ2, and
Adrβ3) in eWAT, iWAT, and BAT.
Our new data reveal that TOX3 in POMC neurons orchestrates a coordinated
regulation of both sympathetic tone and target tissue sensitivity. In PTKO mice, the
reduction in BAT NE levels and turnover was accompanied by a downregulation of
Adrβ1, Adrβ2, and Adrβ3 mRNA (Figure R2.3c). Conversely, TOX3 overexpression
(PTOE) increased Adrβ2 and Adrβ3 mRNA expression (Figure R2.3f). These
findings demonstrate that the TOX3-POMC axis likely modulates not only
neurotransmitter availability but also the adrenergic responsiveness of the target tissue.
Notably, β-adrenergic receptor expression remained unchanged in eWAT and iWAT
(Figure R2.3a,b; 3d,e), highlighting the specificity of this regulation to BAT.
Together with our functional rescue experiment using a β3-AR selective agonist
(Figure 5f-k), these results establish a dual-level mechanism: TOX3 in POMC
neurons maintains both the sympathetic drive to BAT and the intrinsic adrenergic
signaling capacity of the tissue itself. These data have been incorporated into the
revised manuscript.

7. The study only confirms the protective role of the sympathetic nervous system in
TOX3-mediated effects in brown adipose tissue (BAT) using 6-hydroxydopamine
hydrobromide (6-OHDA). The authors should also evaluate the effects of sympathetic
inhibition in white adipose tissue (WAT) before concluding that the protective effect is
specifically mediated via BAT.
Response: Thank you for raising this important point, which prompted us to perform
the critical experiment you suggested. To specifically evaluate the role of sympathetic
innervation in WAT, we performed bilateral, local microinjections of 6-OHDA into
both the eWAT and iWAT depots of control and PTOE mice.
The results showed that, following chemical denervation of eWAT and iWAT (Figure
R2.4a-c), PTOE mice continued to exhibit a lower body weight than control mice
(Figure R2.4d), along with reduced fat mass and increased lean mass composition
(Figure R2.4e). Combined with our BAT denervation results, these data provide
strong functional evidence that sympathetic innervation of BAT is the primary and
necessary efferent pathway through which elevated TOX3 in POMC neurons exerts
its protective effect against weight gain.
Figure R2.4 NE content in eWAT (a), iWAT (b), and BAT (c) of Pomc-Cre mice
injected with AAV-GFP or AAV-Tox3, followed by bilateral injection of either saline
or 6-OHDA into both eWAT and iWAT. (d) Body weight of Control and PTOE mice 4
weeks after 6-OHDA injection. (e) Mass composition of Control and PTOE mice 4
weeks after 6-OHDA injection.
It is noteworthy that, although TOX3 overexpression increased NE content in WAT
depots (See Supplementary Figure 10d), the denervation experiment indicates that this
modulation alone is not sufficient to drive the core body weight phenotype under our
experimental conditions. Sympathetic tone to WAT may play a modulatory role but
does not appear to be the dominant mediator of the TOX3-dependent effect on
whole-body energy balance.
Thus, our data supports a model in which TOX3 in POMC neurons preferentially
enhances sympathetic output to BAT. The recruited BAT then acts as the primary
driver of increased energy expenditure, outweighing the relative contribution of
sympathetic-mediated effects in WAT to the overall metabolic phenotype.
We have updated the Methods, Results and Discussion sections to include these new
WAT denervation data and to refine our conclusion accordingly: Notably, although
TOX3 overexpression also increased NE content in WAT depots, sympathetic
denervation experiments indicate that this modulation alone is not sufficient to drive
the core body weight phenotype under our experimental conditions. Thus, while
sympathetic tone to WAT may exert a modulatory role, it does not appear to be the
dominant mediator of TOX3-dpendent regulation of whole-body energy balance.
Instead, our data support a model in which TOX3 in POMC neurons preferentially
enhances sympathetic output to BAT. The BAT then acts as the primary driver of
increased energy expenditure, outweighing the relative contribution of
sympathetic-mediated effects in WAT to the overall metabolic phenotype.

some of the adipose data were associations, meaning the author cannot exclude the
effect of TOX3/POMC on extra-adipose tissues. The systemic use of β3-adrenergic

Response: Thank you for this insightful suggestion. As recommended, we have
performed qPCR analysis to profile the expression of key metabolic genes in the liver
(Cd36, Srebf1, Fasn, Acaca, Cpt1α, Cpt2, Apob, Mttp) and skeletal muscle (Cd36,

We found that PTKO mice exhibited significantly higher mRNA levels

compared to LoxP controls, while no significant changes were observed in skeletal

We revised our Discussion section as follows: However, several important questions
remain unanswered, including whether hypothalamic POMC neuron TOX3 directly
modulates other peripheral metabolic processes - such as hepatic gluconeogenesis,
hepatic lipid metabolism, pancreatic endocrine function, and skeletal muscle
metabolism - as well as the molecular mechanisms underlying these potential effects.

Reviewer #3:
The manuscript by Qin Tang, Juan Pang and Jinhang Zhang et al. presents a
compelling and well-designed study that significantly advances the understanding of
central regulation of energy homeostasis. The authors provide robust evidence
identifying TOX3 as a critical and previously overlooked metabolic regulator
specifically within POMC neurons. Using genetic models, the authors show that
TOX3 loss exacerbates diet-induced obesity, while its overexpression improves
metabolism via a post-translational mechanism involving PTEN degradation and
enhanced AKT signaling. The findings reveal a neuron-specific role for TOX3 in
energy homeostasis and suggest its potential as a therapeutic target for metabolic
disorders. However, there are some experiments and descriptions need to be
improved.
Response: Thank you for your constructive review and positive assessment of our
study on TOX3 in POMC neurons and energy homeostasis. Your constructive
feedback is highly valuable. In response, we have conducted additional experiments,
analyses, and revisions to address each point directly. Below, we provide
point-by-point responses and outline the changes made in the revised manuscript.
Major concerns:
1. The authors should discuss the apparent discrepancy wherein POMC
neuron-specific TOX3 ablation shows no phenotype on a chow diet (CD), despite the
significant metabolic effect observed upon broader hypothalamic TOX3 knockdown
under the same conditions. Please clarify whether this suggests that TOX3 in
non-POMC hypothalamic neurons is responsible for the metabolic regulation
observed under CD, and how this aligns with the proposed POMC-specific role for
TOX3.
Response: We appreciate the opportunity to clarify this apparent discrepancy, which
stems from a key difference in the experimental conditions that we may not have
emphasized sufficiently.
The significant metabolic effect following broader hypothalamic Tox3 knockdown
was specifically observed under high-fat diet (HFD) feeding (see Figure 1). In
contrast, the POMC neuron-specific ablation was tested on a CD, where we did not
observe a metabolic phenotype.
However, a critical and consistent finding that further strengthens our conclusion is
that under HFD conditions, the POMC neuron-specific Tox3 knockout (see Figure 2)
recapitulates the key metabolic phenotypes observed with the broader hypothalamic
knockdown. This demonstrates that Tox3 in POMC neurons is both necessary and
sufficient to mediate the metabolic effects observed under dietary challenge.
Therefore, the absence of a phenotype in the POMC-specific KO mice on CD cannot
be directly compared to the effects of global hypothalamic knockdown, as the latter
was assessed under metabolically challenged (HFD) conditions. The cell-type-specific
effects are diet-context dependent. We fully agree that non-POMC hypothalamic
neurons might also be involved in Tox3-dependent metabolic regulation, especially
under dietary stress. This view is consistent with our expression data showing Tox3 in
other neuronal populations (See Figure S2a) and with the known complexity of
hypothalamic energy balance circuits.
We have revised the Discussion to explicitly acknowledge that Tox3 likely functions
in a cell-type- and context-specific manner, and that its role in non-POMC
neurons—particularly under metabolic challenge—deserves future investigation:
although we have comprehensively characterized TOX3 expression and function in
POMC and AgRP neurons, it is also expressed in other hypothalamic neuronal
populations. Moreover, while minimal Tox3 expression was detected in tanycytes,
astrocytes, and microglia, public scRNA-seq datasets indicate that Tox3 is enriched in
oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs), suggesting a potential role in glial biology.
The physiological relevance of TOX3 in these other neuronal and non-neuronal cell
types, particularly under metabolic challenge, represents an important avenue for
future research.
2. It would also be important to know the phenotypic effects of overexpressing TOX3
in POMC neurons under chow diet conditions, to fully elucidate its physiological role
without the confounder of dietary stress.
Response: Thank you for this important suggestion. As suggested, we overexpressed
TOX3 specifically in ARC POMC neurons of Pomc-Cre mice maintained on a
standard chow diet (CD).
Our results showed that, under CD conditions, TOX3 overexpression in POMC
neurons did not significantly affect body weight, body composition (fat and lean
mass), organ weights (liver and adipose depots), serum lipid profiles, glucose
tolerance, or insulin sensitivity (Figure R3.1a-j). This indicates that in the absence of
a metabolic challenge such as a HFD, elevated TOX3 expression in POMC neurons
does not exert a pronounced effect on systemic energy homeostasis. These data have
been included as a Supplementary Figure in the revised manuscript, and the
corresponding Results and figure legends have been updated accordingly.

5. Evidence demonstrating the efficacy of 6-OHDA-mediated sympathetic denervation

we directly measured norepinephrine (NE) content in eWAT, iWAT, and BAT

Our results show that NE levels in eWAT and iWAT were not significantly altered by

6-OHDA-treated group (Figure R3.3c).

POMC neurons, with no significant difference observed in non-POMC neurons
(Figure R3.4c). These results confirm the cell-type specificity of our approach. These
quantitative results have been included in the revised manuscript.

### Reviewer 1

The authors have only partly addressed the concerns of this reviewer. The main limitations about the genetic model used and the approaches to demonstrate deletion/overexpression in mature POMC neurons still stand.
Concerning the demonstration that the manipulation impact also adult POMC neurons, for figure S2A, S2F and S6C, instead of using fluorescence of POMC-Cre Ai9 mice, please perform staining for POMC protein or mRNA in combination with Tox3 mRNA staining. As already mentioned, POMC-Cre Ai9 label all POMC-lineage cells. The argument used by the authors that other studies have used this genetic approach to reveal deletion (or overexpression) in POMC cells, does not make the approach correct.
In the manuscript, it needs to be clear for the reader that the genetic model used does not allow specific deletion only in POMC neurons. The authors need to consider using terms like POMC-lineage cells throughout the manuscript.
For the energy expenditure data throughout the manuscript: as there are differences in body weight, please also use ANCOVA for EE analysis (for details please see PMID: 22205519 and PMID: 34489606).

### Reviewer 2

In the revision, the authors have addressed most of my comments and as a result, the manuscript has improved from its previous version.
A remaining issue is that the authors explained that the difference in the degree of obesity between the loss-of-function and gain-of-function models is due to the different timing of high-fat diet exposure relative to the gene manipulation. The authors should clarify the rationale for initiating HFD feeding before TOX3 overexpression in the gain-of-function model, rather than overexpressing TOX3 prior to HFD challenge, which would be more comparable with the loss-of-function studies.

### Reviewer 3

The authors have fully addressed all my previous concerns. I have no further questions and recommend acceptance.
